speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on an urgent and pressing matter. It is urgent, because every day that goes by means more waste of money. The education department of the province of British Columbia has conducted a massive test of over 90,000 British Columbia school children in grades four, eight and twelve, and has determined that their knowledge of metric is sadly lacking. DISASTERS
subsubtopic: SINKING OF "OCEAN RANGER"-QUERY RESPECTING MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF OFFSHORE DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. As the tragedy of the Ocean Ranger and the tragic loss of lives unfolds, there is obvious confusion over jurisdiction between the federal, provincial and United States governments. Would the minister agree that this accentuates the need for responsible ministers in these three jurisdictions to sit down now and work out a de facto management system for control and safety of offshore drilling activity, to prevent any further loss of lives?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):

subsubtopic: SINKING OF "OCEAN RANGER"-QUERY RESPECTING MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF OFFSHORE DEVELOPMENT

I would argue, however, that the third jurisdiction, the United States government, should not be a party to the discussions relating to the management of the Canadian offshore. I agree with the hon. member it is important that we arrive at a negotiated agreement on the management of resources and revenue sharing.

subtopic: UNITED STATES ROLE IN SAFETY CERTIFICATION
UNITED STATES ROLE IN SAFETY CERTIFICATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the United States government will not be involved in a meaningful de facto way in the operations of offshore drilling rigs in waters which may not be territorial but have been claimed for us under our economic management zones, why was an American coastguard inspection team going to the rig to try to update a certificate of safety which had a two-year validity period and evidently was two months overdue? If there is not some part for them also, what are we supposed to be doing in relation to the safety of oil rigs?
Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and
Resources): Madam Speaker, I remind the hon. member that beyond our 12-mile limit, our territorial waters, we are in international waters, and that Canada has a responsibility for fisheries and the management of resources, and the countries in which the ships or drilling rigs are registered also have responsibility under the Canada Shipping Act and under international conventions with regard to the flag of registry of those installations, whether they are ships or drilling rigs. Thus, there is a United States involvement because this particular drilling rig was under the American flag.

subtopic: DEPARTMENTAL RESPONSIBILITY
DEPARTMENTAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is really directed to the Minister of Transport.
Without arguing the point of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the fact there is a third jurisdiction involved outside territorial waters, the government of the United States, I direct my question to the minister concerning apparent confusion of jurisdiction within departments. I should like the minister to explain just what is his responsibility as Minister of Transport for the safe operation of drilling rigs in Canadian waters, especially in view of the fact that a recent report on the evaluation of search and rescue, dated February 1, 1982, made no mention of offshore drilling activity and highlighted jurisdictional problems within departments. At page 21, referring to departmental responsibility, it reads:
The resultant split in the functional responsibilities for safety within the CCG does not appear to the team-
That is the study team.
-to be an effective way to use resources.
At page 30 it indicates even more directly:
Finally, in the absence of a convincing demonstration that current marine response capability is inadequate and that better marine postures are not feasible-
And I interject here that the whole tenor of this is marine response for pleasure craft and fishermen, and not a word about offshore activity.
-the team would give lowest priority to the provision of new resources for marine response.
In view of this current report which is being studied and is supposed to go to cabinet on March 17, 1982, will the minister start to exercise some responsibility, so that deaths in the future are prevented and that someone takes control to save Canadian lives and starts to direct attention to the reality out there, rather than worrying about offshore pleasure craft and/or just fishermen?

subtopic: DEPARTMENTAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the Canada Shipping Act my department has no jurisdiction over foreign-registered ships past the 12-mile zone; that is pretty fundamental. Thus, as Minister of Transport, I cannot go and inspect rigs or ships in that area.
With respect to seaworthiness of ships or rigs, a general principle in marine transportation, as well as in air transportation, is to accept the system of the foreign country involved. If my hon. friend wants to read the Dubin report, for example, Mr. Justice Dubin repeatedly recommended that we should not try to second-guess the system of another country, particularly if it is one that is as evolved as the United States of America is in this matter. The principle of reciprocity applies here in matters of marine transportation as well as in matters of air transportation.

Madam Speaker, my question is also to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Yesterday he indicated to the House that the safety of workers on ocean rigs fell under federal jurisdiction and was exercised under the Canada Oil and Gas Act. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is related to a question asked a moment ago, and it is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The minister knows that Canadian manufacturers of mining equipment have been quickly losing ground to foreign competitors in supplying our rapidly growing demand for mining equipment. In fact he knows that between 1970 and 1980 the percentage of Canadian-manufactured mining equipment dropped from over 70 per cent to a mere 29 per cent, giving rise to a $167 million trade deficit in 1980, compared to only a $48 million trade deficit a decade earlier.
Will the minister explain why his government has allowed the Canadian content in mining equipment to slip to rock bottom levels over the past ten years? Madam Speaker, it is true that in 1980 Canada produced $342 million worth of mining equipment and imported $372.4 million worth. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I gave you notice that I wished to raise a question of privilege with respect to the statements made in the House yesterday by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), as reported at pages 14996-7 of Hansard, and a subsequent press release dated February 15, 1982 under the authority of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde).
Yesterday in the House, as reported at page 14996 of Hansard, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) raised a point of order because an announcement was to be made that afternoon establishing a formal inquiry into the Hibernia matter and was not being made properly, that is, in the House of Commons, giving hon. members an opportunity for reply.
At page 14997 of Hansard, after an intervention by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the President of the Privy Council said:
-Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has just told me there will be no announcement today. Under the circumstances, there is no problem.
Later yesterday afternoon, after a press conference, Members of Parliament received a copy of a press release which reads as follows:
Transport Minister Jean-Luc Pepin and Energy Minister Marc Lalonde today announced that the federal government will hold a formal inquiry to investigate all aspects of the loss of the drilling rig Ocean Ranger off Newfoundland early today.
February 16, 1982

I raise this question of privilege in a reluctant way, Madam Speaker, because in my short experience in the House I have found the President of the Privy Council to be an honest, straightforward, honourable member. Nevertheless, I take the opportunity to raise this question of privilege so that he can clarify his statement to the House. His statement was clearly misleading: it clearly said that there would be no announcement. Then suddenly, two hours later, there was an announcement. 1 will send it up to you so that you can see it for yourself.
My question is that I and perhaps other hon. members, perhaps inadvertently, have been misled by the statement made by the President of the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRIVILEGE
subsubtopic: MR. WADDELL-ANNOUNCEMENT OF COMMISSION OF INQUIRY INTO SINKING OF "OCEAN RANGER" OIL RIG
speechtext:
Unless the hon. member tells the House that he was intentionally misled by the House he does not have a question of privilege. If he feels that he might have been misled inadvertently, then of course he knows that there is no foundation for a question of privilege. If the press release, in his view, was not in conformity with statements made in the House, that is a debatable question and, of course, he may debate it. Even if the hon. member wanted me to look at all of these statements to determine whether there were discrepancies in them, it is not for the Chair to establish discrepancies.
If these statements, in the mind of the hon. member, do not seem to conform with what was said in the House, unless he is prepared to tell me that the minister has intentionally misled him-and he has not done that-I cannot find the basis for a question of privilege.

subtopic: RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES AND TO PROVIDE

speechtext:
On the Order: Government Orders:

Whole of Bill C-93, to amend the statute law relating to certain taxes and to provide other authority for the raising of funds.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
subtopic: RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES AND TO PROVIDE
speechtext:
On Wednesday, February 10, 1982, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) raised a point of order in relation to Bill C-93, to amend the statute law relating to certain taxes and to provide other authority for the raising of funds. The hon. member expressed concern that the bill contained matters based on ways and means motions and other matters of substance, namely, the authority to borrow money. The hon. member claimed that for that reason the bill is an omnibus bill. It was further argued that each of the two features of the bill calls for two different modes of proceeding through the legislative process.
As hon. members will recall, the practice prior to 1969 was to include a provision for borrowing authority in supply bills. Such bills were discussed under a different supply procedure, giving hon. members ample opportunity to debate all aspects of those bills. This procedure was changed with the adoption of the new supply procedures currently in effect which introduced certain limitations into that process. It was for this reason that my predecessor ruled in favour of removing the borrowing provisions from supply bills.
The same limitations in debate do not prevail under the ways and means procedures. Recently the borrowing provisions were included in bills based on ways and means motions, which 1 do not find objectionable. As I indicated to the House on January 19, 1981, I have no quarrel with the practice of combining in the same bill taxation matters based on ways and means motion with the borrowing authority, provided the notice provision was respected. In the case of Bill C-93, this requirement has been met, I can find no objection to the bill being proceeded with, and I so rule.

that Bill C-93, to amend the statute law relating to certain

February 16, 1982
Taxation
taxes and to provide other authority for the raising of funds, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Madam Speaker, this bill implements a number of commitments which had been made to the energy producing provinces. The bill also provides for several technical changes in the federal excise tax system and, as you just said, its purpose is also to obtain new borrowing powers for the fiscal year 1982-83.
Hon. members will recall that last fall, the Government of Canada entered into agreements with Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia on the pricing of oil and natural gas and the sharing of revenue from those resources. The five-year agreements established a price scale for oil and natural gas and provided a sound basis for achieving Canada's energy goals. The bill before the House today consists of three parts. In the first part, the government is seeking borrowing authority for the fiscal year 1982-83. Part II amends the Excise Tax Act by implementing several changes resulting from the energy agreements, as well as technical changes in the federal sales tax system. Part III of the bill amends the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act according to the agreement concluded by the Government of Canada and the oil producing provinces.
Thus, in the first part, the government is seeking borrowing authority for $6.6 billion. Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that all unused borrowing authority, granted under the Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 and in excess of $3 billion, will lapse on March 31, 1982. Without new borrowing powers, the government will be unable to obtain the necessary funds to meet its financial requirements for 1982-83. The new borrowing authority for $6.6 billion will cover budgetary and nonbudgetary financial requirements for 1982-83 as estimated in the budget tabled in the House last November. We are seeking borrowing powers now so as to have the authority when the new fiscal year starts on April 1, 1982.
Since this borrowing authority bill is directly connected with the budget, I think it would be useful to review the budget's main objectives in light of the economic situation and thus provide a background for evaluating the merits of the bill. The budget's main theme, as hon. members will recall, was that rapidly rising inflation was the main problem in our economy. Inflation tends to push up interest rates, destroy investor confidence and generally slow down economic activity. This in turn leads to a number of problems: rising unemployment, erosion of real income and borrowers saddled with the burden of ever-increasing interest rates. This has indeed been confirmed by the phenomena we have been seeing in Canada; during the past years inflation has accelerated while labour market conditions have failed to improve. To cope with these problems, the government decided to adopt its present policy of waging a persistent battle against inflation. We must reduce inflation if we want our country to realize its growth potential.
The budget has stressed the need for gradually and substantially reducing the government's deficit. With a lower deficit, the government will be able to cut back its demands on the capital markets and leave more room for other borrowers, while relieving pressure on interest rates. The next tax and expenditure control measures set forth in the budget will prevent the deficit from rising to intolerable levels, thus reflecting the government's commitment to fiscal restraint. I recall, Mr. Speaker, that the government has been able to reduce its cash requirements while at the same time providing tax cuts for the vast majority of Canadian citizens. A substantial drop in marginal income tax rates, changes in the federal tax rebate system and continued indexation of individual income tax-all these measures have resulted in lower taxes for most Canadians. Of course, Canadians who have benefited from various tax exemptions, especially those in the higher income bracket, and also some of the large corporations will be paying more taxes as a result of the budget. However, some tax increases were necessary, and they are mostly affecting those Canadians who are best able to absorb them.
The government has also made an effort to restrict growth of government expenditures. It is always difficult to apply such restrictions, especially at a time when the economy is flagging, since government programs tend to meet a wide range of both social and economic needs which are all equally important. Thus, while keeping its expenditures within reasonable limits, the government did not want to make indiscriminate cuts in its budget. The need for a firm but fair policy to fight against inflation, like the one adopted by the government, has become even more apparent in the light of the events that have taken place since the budget was tabled in this House. Inflation rates similar to those experienced last year are keeping interest rates at high levels and causing a pronounced slump in economic activity. Other countries are having to cope with the same problems, and the recession has also affected the United States, Great Britain, Germany, France and Japan. Like Canada, and almost without exception, these countries have admitted that inflation was at the root of their problems, and they have maintained anti-inflationary tax and monetary policies.
In the United States, where the impact of energy prices has been cushioned more quickly than in Canada, inflation has already started to slow down. Of course, this means that with a higher rate of inflation in Canada, our industry is beginning to be less competitive than American companies. We must therefore make every effort to check inflation, otherwise the Canadian industry will lose some of its export markets for good, all the more as further energy price increases are expected in Canada.
Because of higher unemployment in recent months, certain critics have asked the government to provide massive economic incentives. However, they take no heed of the lessons of the recent past which show that there is no quick answer to such

basic problems as inflation. These critics would have the government show substantial deficits, unmindful of the consequences that this would have on inflation and on already excessive interest rates. This would mean that the government would have to borrow more money on capital markets, which would create additional upward pressures on interest rates. These same critics reply that this would not necessarily occur since the Bank of Canada can increase the money supply and devaluate the Canadian dollar. However, the government believes, as we have often repeated, that such a policy is shortsighted. It would lead inevitably to a much higher rate of inflation, to higher interest rates and to worse unemployment than is now the case.
The reasonable solution is the one we have chosen. We must not only look at today's figures, but we must also lay the foundations of tomorrow's economy. As I have stated, Mr. Speaker, budgetary and non-budgetary financial requirements for 1982-83 amount to a total of $6.6 billion. In addition to forecast financial requirements, we shall need as usual some margin for contingencies resulting for instance, from exchange operations. In the last few years, this contingency fund has fluctuated around the figure of $3 billion and has normally been added to the total borrowing authority requested. This year, however, these $3 billion or what remains of the borrowing authority for 1981-82 if the difference is lower than $3 billion will not lapse automatically at the end of the fiscal year and may therefore be carried forward. The amount carried forward will therefore represent the contingency margin required for the 1982-83 fiscal year.
The provision to the effect that the government may borrow and repay amounts in a foreign currency is of a technical nature. It was included in the last four borrowing authority bills. Throughout the years, Canada has borrowed and repaid amounts in a number of foreign currencies. This provision was, however, added in the last few years to confirm the right of Canada to borrow any amount in foreign currencies. The government intends to introduce in the near future a bill to amend the Financial Administration Act, including a provision to define the power of the government to borrow and repay any amount in foreign currencies.
Once the amendment has been introduced and passed by Parliament, there will be no need for that kind of provision.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment briefly on government borrowing operations since the beginning of the current Fiscal year, and the extent of borrowing authorities that have been used. The act that granted borrowing authority for 1981-82 brought new borrowing authority for $14 billion. Hon. members will recall that it was given royal assent on April 8, 1981. From April 8, 1981 to February 1, 1982, the government raised a total of $9,700 million in new funds on the domestic markets. Of that total, $9,600 million came from
Taxation
Canada Savings Bonds and $2 billion from marketable bonds, while net redemptions of treasury bonds lowered by $1,900 million the amounts borrowed that I have just been referring to.
The government raised $300 million on foreign markets through private placement of an issue with the Saudi Arabian monetary authority. Drawings had been made earlier in the year on our renewable line of credit with Canadian banks, but they were all repaid. There is currently no drawing in process on that line of credit nor those opened with U.S. and international banks. Taking into account the bond issue in foreign currencies, by February 1, the government will have used $10,100 million of borrowing authority, leaving an unused balance of $3,900 million. This summary of borrowing operations of the current balance of borrowing authorities should provide hon. members with the information needed for their assessment of this first part of the legislation. Clearly we will have an opportunity, during later discussions, to answer more precise questions and supply further data on these various operations, as called for in the Standing Orders, at a later stage of our proceedings.
Part II of the legislation, as I said in my opening remarks, implements the first ways and means motion, dealing with the Excise Tax Act, which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) brought down in his budget on November 12, 1981. It provides for three technical amendments concerning the federal sales tax, and also proposes changes to the natural gas and natural gas liquids tax. The hon. members and the public had an opportunity to hear wide discussion of the principles underlying the energy policy of the government of Canada. They are also aware that, thanks to the remarkable work of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), the Canadian government reached an agreement with the main oil producing provinces. The agreements and understandings required certain amendments to the oil and gas taxes, and further to the income tax on oil revenues.
In the bill, federal tax on natural gas exports has been removed, except on natural gas from Canada lands. The zero rate will be in effect during the period from October I, 1981, until December 31, 1986; in other words, for the duration of the agreements concluded with the producing provinces. The bill also provides for refunding tax on ethane exported during that period. The tax on domestic sales of natural gas will be set in such a way that the wholesale price including tax and cost of transportation to wholesalers in Toronto is about 65 per cent of the average price paid for crude oil by refiners in Toronto. This will be a strong incentive for conversion to natural gas, while consumers already using natural gas will continue to enjoy substantial benefits.
As of January 1, 1982, the tax rate was 42 cents per gigajoule, and it was raised to 63 cents per gigajoule on February 1, 1982. The legislation as it stands now provides for a rate of 56 cents per gigajoule for the entire year. Thus, the

February 16, 1982
Taxation
rate will largely depend on the blended oil price, which in turn varies according to the international price of oil. The following technical changes have been made in the sales tax system. First of all, the excise tax rate has been lowered on wines of all kinds containing not more than 1.2 per cent absolute ethyl alcohol by volume. Small manufacturers can apply for refunds of sales tax paid on machines and equipment purchased for use in their manufacturing operations.
Finally, the penalty on default of payment of federal sales and excise tax will be raised from 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent per month. Hon. members will recall that in his last budget, the Minister of Finance announced a major change in the sales tax system, namely, that the tax would be applied at the wholesale instead of at the manufacturer's level. This change in the Canadian sales tax system will be considered by hon. members at a later date. In fact, last week, the Minister of Finance said that when the bill was tabled we would have an opportunity to discuss in greater detail all the aspects of this major change in the application of the federal tax. Part III of the bill amends the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act. The tax on oil and gas production revenue which was introduced in the National Energy Program on October 28, 1980, will, or rather has been raised from 8 per cent to 16 per cent as of January 1, 1982. However, taxpayers will be able to take advantage of a new resource deduction on all oil and gas production revenue subject to this tax.
The bill also contains a provision allowing for reduction of tax on synthetic oil production projects during the initial years of production. The bill also provides for a tax on incremental oil revenue, which will be applied to production of oil found before 1981. As of January, 1982, this tax will be 50 per cent of incremental revenue, after deduction of related Crown royalties. Incremental revenue occurs because prices for old oil are higher than the prices established in the National Energy Program announced in 1980. Revenue thus taxed will be exempt from income tax. In addition the same tax will be reduced with respect to wells producing less than 20 barrels per month. This reduction, also known as the adjustment for low productivity wells, will be of substantial benefit to producers in Saskatchewan, where many such wells exist.
Mr. Speaker, the bill also includes several minor technical changes designed to lessen the impact of the tax on oil and natural gas revenue. Although removal of the export tax on natural gas will reduce revenue drawn from this resource, all changes included in the energy agreements concluded with the producing provinces will increase revenue received under the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act. Thus, the net effect of all these changes will be to reduce the government's financial requirements in the future. The bill will also help bring about a more equitable distribution of the revenue generated by oil and gas production and will provide the industry with sufficient liquid assets while removing the uncertainty that existed
before the energy agreements with the provinces were finalized.
In the final instance, Mr. Speaker, the bill constitutes a major component of the government's long-term financial plan, and one of its major aspects as it relates to the energy agreements signed with the producing provinces. I believe that this bill, which implements a number of fiscal changes that have been approved by the provinces and whose purpose is also to seek borrowing authority for the next fiscal year, is fully deserving of the support of this House.

We as Canadian taxpayers were asked to support a 19.5 per cent interest rate on Canada Savings Bonds. In October, before the Canada Savings Bonds campaign was well along, we asked in this House whether the rate could be changed. We asked if it could be reduced because, we said, otherwise it would cause tremendous problems. The minister said it could not be reduced. He kept the interest rate at 19.5 per cent. That Canada Savings Bonds move created an enormous debt management nightmare. Canada Savings Bonds were issued in 1978, 1979, 1980 and 1981 and, as a result, the total amount outstanding is now about $20 billion. We had a policy-and this goes back five or six years-of reducing reliance on Canada Savings Bonds in over-all debt management operations because it is effectively demand money, and I believe it was in 1979 that the Conservative government got into a box because of the debt management problem left to it by the Liberal governments of previous years. During the period from, I believe, 1975, the proportion of Canada Savings Bonds to the national debt dropped from 38 per cent to 20 per cent. It got down to a more manageable figure. However, what has happened as a result of the debacle last fall? The proportion of Canada Savings Bonds as a percentage of the over-all debt outstanding is now back up to 38 per cent. We are back to where we started. Canada Savings Bonds are costing us 19.5 per cent and will present to future governments a tremendous debt management problem as they try to manage this great big lump which will have to be renewed each year, year in and year out, at a very substantial cost to the taxpayers of this country. 1 was hoping the minister would respond to that concern. In the 1980 budget these two taxes, the excise tax on natural gas and the production tax-the PGRT-were introduced. At that time members of the Conservative Party opposed those taxes. We said they would be very damaging to the future outlook for energy in this country. We said that the energy security of this country would be severely damaged by the extent of those taxes. Drilling completions are down 26 per cent from 1980 to 1981; exploration spending is down 22 per cent from 1980 to 1981; production per day is down a small amount, 100,000 barrels per day. The impact of this lower spending on exploration and drilling will be seen perhaps not this year, but two, three, four or five years from now. Future generations will suffer from the shortcomings of these policies.
The reason for the setback in the development of the industry is that the cash flow of the industry has dropped by 35 per cent. Money that had previously been spent to develop future natural resources has been translated into government spending dollars which have been wasted. It is just throwing good money after bad with this 22 per cent increase in spending.

1 should like to quote some comments made by the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I think it is important that we understand why it is necessary to cut back on government borrowing-so that we can free up the resources of the country that the private sector may borrow. The Governor of the bank said that restraint on investment is felt through various channels, one of which is that the fiscal deficit absorbed savings that could otherwise be channelled by financial markets into financing the expansion of plant and equipment. He said that this could militate against the increases in productivity and income that capital formation makes possible.
What he is really saying, Mr. Speaker, is that borrowing by the private sector-individuals, small, medium and large-sized companies-enables those companies to make themselves more competitive, more productive, more able to employ people and more able to create jobs in this country. Surely the government understands the importance of creating jobs when there are 1.1 million people out of work today. Business survives on longterm capital.
We heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) talk about the importance of lower cost and stable capital to the agricultural community. Those same words can be used in respect of any sector of the economy. What has happened in
Taxation
recent years, because huge deficits were built up by the government, is that the stability, availability and cost of long-term capital has been thrown totally out of whack. If businessmen, farmers, fishermen and individuals do not have access to capital, it will make for a very disruptive economy.
In order to draw this down to a level which anyone in the House can understand, today we heard complaints about the fact that mortgage money is not available for 20 or 25-year terms. It is my understanding that there are only three institutions which will make five-year money available in the form of mortgages for the purchase of homes. If Canadians are faced with the possibility of buying homes but not knowing what the mortgage rate will be in one year or two years, it is similar to playing Russian roulette; it is a large crap shoot in Las Vegas. They do not know what will be the cost of their biggest asset.
This is why we must have stability in the financial markets of the country. It is not big business people who suffer in this regard; it is people who borrow to purchase homes, or small businessmen who must finance businesses which provide employment for people. If they do not have the benefit of stable financial markets, it will make a very difficult economic environment within which to operate. The real crunch is on farmers, fishermen, small-business men and home owners. We should be concerned about those people. It is very clear to them why the Conservative Party has stressed the importance of keeping the federal government deficit within the bounds of the financial markets of the country and within its financial capacity. Clearly it has not done so for a number of years.
I should like to talk about one other aspect of federal government deficits, and that is its impact upon future generations. We all know that a deficit is simply a deferral of taxes. The government has expenditures of some $70 billion and it has revenues coming in of $57 billion. Clearly tax revenues are not sufficient to cover spending, thus $13 billion of deficit is borrowed. Is it lost forever? Not on your life! What happens when $13 billion is borrowed this year at 15 per cent per annum? In five years' time, in 1987, it will become $26 billion; by 1992 it will become $52 billion; by 1997 it will become $104 billion. One could apply that calculation to next year's deficit or the deficit of the year after. They pile up one on top of the other. Some of us who are in the House today may not be around in the year 2000 to pay the load of these deferred taxes; it will be our children who will pay. The legacy we are leaving for younger people, who are having a hard enough time finding jobs because of the shortcomings of government policy, is that they will be suffering from the shortcomings of the same policy in 1995, 2005, and so on. This is why we must get on top of the deficits of today.
Again I ask the minister why the government is so casual about its attitude toward deficit and spending control. I looked at the home owner renewal program of the recent budget wherein the government very generously provided a guarantee for a home owner if he does not have sufficient income to pay his mortgage payments because his payments are more than 30 per cent of his income. The government said that it would provide a guarantee so that he could borrow. 1 think Canadi-

ans are too smart for this. They have seen the government doing it year in and year out, and they have seen the impact of a government which now pays $1 in $5 in interest. They know that if they defer some of their interest payments for one, two, three, Five or ten years at 15 per cent, 18 per cent or 20 per cent, the same thing will happen to them. But they understand why the government is so casual in presenting such a program; it is the manner in which the government has lived for the last ten years. It encourages the home owner to put himself more and more into debt, as has the government.
I think this is the best illustration we can give to government of why it is wrong to present a bail-out program for individual home owners. Surely it should look no further than at what happened with its own financial position before asking individual home owners to put themselves in the same financial position by deferring debt and expenses for years into the future and by letting them compound at 15 per cent or 20 per cent per annum. It is criminal to ask Canadians to do this. I do not think any home owner will be too anxious to take this snake oil because they know the results.
I should like to talk about some of the problems we are facing and about some of the ways of solving them. We on this side of the House have been asked on a number of occasions what we would do differently or how we would attack the problems of today. I think the difference becomes clearer every day. On many occasions I have referred to increasing attempts by the Liberal government to gain more and more control or power over the big levers of the economy. We have seen how pushing the economy into the dirt, raising interest rates to enormously high levels and forcing cutbacks in the economy have forced people into positions where they must come to the government to ask for help and for programs to tide them over these very difficult times. We do not want to see it done that way. We want to reverse the direction we have been going in recent years. We want to make a change which will return spending power to Canadians and will release the tremendous energy of the free enterprise system. We have confidence in the free enterprise system.
How can we do this? How can we come up with a way which will lead to a reduction in inflation, to an increase in growth in the economy and to more job creation? There are no perfect solutions or comparisons, but I should like to look at what happened in Japan and Germany for some inspiration. During the 1970s, these two countries had the strongest currencies and the lowest levels of inflation of any industrialized country in the world. This is no real surprise because those two factors are mutually supportive. We know that a strong currency is a sign of good government. Canada by contrast has seen its currency drop from a value of $1.03 in 1976 in terms of the United States dollar to 80 cents in the current market. We also saw last year, in contrast to these other currencies, that Canada suffered a massive capital outflow, some six times the levels of the 1970s. I should point out that a large part of that outflow was dynamic equity capital, the capital that creates jobs. It is the entrepreneurial, risk-taking capital that has left the country. To offset that Canada has had to put up
interest rates two or three percentage points higher than they should be to attract not the entrepreneurial capital but fixed income. This is passive capital, the capital that does not create jobs anywhere near the extent the risk-taking capital does, the capital that has left the country.
The reason for the outflow of this capital is federal government policy that has been in place for the past two years. We have seen the energy program and what that has done for the country. We have seen the tremendous lack of confidence which investors, businessmen and individuals have in this government on the policies it has been pursuing over the past two years. We have seen the unfriendly attitude of this government toward risk-takers, and capital formation has forced that money out of the country. As a result a tremendous load has been put on all Canadians. Canada has to keep those intest rates two or three percentage points higher than they need be. That is a tremendous burden, not only upon the people who have been forced to take the money out of the country and upon all Canadians who are financing a business or a mortgage, but also upon large companies that are trying to build major projects. The toll is measured in human suffering. It is measured in the loss of a job, bankruptcy or the renewal of a mortgage at ten or more points higher. In addition to this we have the broad slowdown seen in the economy.
Some people have said let the dollar drop. Some people have said let the dollar go and do not worry about the inflationary aspects of doing that. I say that is the wrong way to go. That is the easy way out. It might shield us from those problems for one or two years, but then we will be back to where we started unless we introduce fundamental policies that will get us back on the rails again.
We need those policies today. We should not give ourselves the short-term palliative of letting the dollar drop and letting interest rates drop. If we do that and the dollar drops as low as 75 cents in terms of the U.S. dollar, then we are faced with having to get interest rates back up. What have we changed? We have changed nothing except for a large increase in costs in the imports that are needed in Canada.
We should introduce some policies to restore the level of confidence in the country that will encourage Canadians and foreigners to bring back that money which they took out over the past year or year and a half. We can then revive our dollar, giving us the flexibility to drop interest rates to the level they should be and so they are more consistent with the economic circumstances in this country. That is the direction we should be going. We should take the pressure off our dollar and have our own made-in-Canada interest policy.
How can we do this? First, we have to maximize the involvement of the private sector. The private sector is the sector in this country that creates jobs. If we look at every statistic in Canada we will see that employment growth in the government sector has been pretty well flat over the last ten years. Growth takes place in the private sector. It is in the private sector now where job creation has dropped out of sight

as a result of all the lay-offs caused by the interest rate policy of this government. We have to avoid the direct massive spending programs which the New Democratic Party would have us introduce. They will lead only to more inflation in this country. Let us encourage the private sector.
Second, we have to recognize the anti-investment nature of this budget. It will continue to push money out of the country. That direction must be reversed. We have to reintroduce some of the incentives that were taken away by the budget, incentives that have performed a valuable role over the past five or ten years.
How do we do that? Again, I have to keep coming back to the runaway spending that we have in this country. If we can cut back a little on government spending, more money will flow to the private sector where it will create more jobs, not more taxes.
Next we have to get on with megaprojects. These projects are tremendously important to all parts of the country. Let us have a positive attitude on the part of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and get these projects moving. He should not sit back and concern himself too much with legal aspects and the nuts and bolts of negotiations. He should be taking the broader view of what these projects can do for Canada.
We have a crisis in housing. In my view we have to reverse four key budget measures which have done so much damage to the housing industry. We should enhance the capital cost allowance. We have to take a look at the Foreign Investment Review Agency. We should try to change the nature of FIRA. The government is playing a schizophrenic role. We have heard from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance. On the one hand, they say we have tremendous capital requirements in this country. On the other hand, they make statements that scare foreign money away. Let us take a look at what our objectives are with foreign investment. We should get our act together. If we have money coming in from other countries, we should bring it in under our terms and encourage it. We should not be discouraging it through these malicious statements being made by members of the government.
Federal-provincial relations in this country are probably at an all-time low today, if they are not already at that point. I would say that is the single, most important element in the lack of confidence of individual Canadians and foreigners who consider investing their money in Canada. When people see that the Government of Canada and the provincial governments cannot get together and agree on some of the basic requirements of this country, people say "Let's try elsewhere". That is one of the reasons so much money left Canada last year.
We have to recognize the tremendous importance and the potential of research and development in this country. Canadians can compete. We have proven ourselves through companies such as Mitel Corporation, Northern Telecom Limited and Canadian General Electric. These companies have competed worldwide.

The same thing is taking place in the United States, Germany, Japan and so on. We have to change that situation.
So, Mr. Speaker, I believe that if we can turn the atmosphere around and increase the confidence level through a combination of these policies, Canadians will start believing in their country again and that we have and can build a future in Canada. We can increase productivity and see a higher value Canadian dollar, which will allow us to drop interest rates. That combination of factors will result in lower interest rates, lower inflation and certainly a much more productive economic environment. That is the direction we have to go. We have to get hold of ourselves to go in that direction, and I think the combination of policies I have set out will allow us to reach that potential.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the reason 1 believe Bill C-93 and the minister's statement are so disappointing, so irresponsible today, is that the bill does nothing to rebuild that sense of confidence which has been so shattered in recent years and which is so necessary if we are to attain that growth. We have to have a return of confidence if we are to see a return of capital into this country. The return of dynamic job-creating capital to Canada would allow us to reduce these painful lay-offs which have been so damaging to our economic future. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with pleasure this afternoon to speak to Bill C-93. I must say that I enjoyed listening to the comments of the lonely cheerleader, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres), as he attempted to pat himself and his party on the back by outlining the positive nature of seeking authority to borrow $6.6 billion. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that while he went on to indicate that the Liberal way of approaching the financial problems facing Canada is the way of reason, I am certain I speak for all members on this side of the House when I say it appears to us that their approach is the way toward economic treason in terms of combating the financial challenges facing us today.
Since this bill, Mr. Speaker, includes three quite separate areas for consideration, and considering the time constraints placed on us, I am going to focus my attention on only one section of the bill, that having to do with the borrowing authority for $6.6 billion. I think anyone who is appreciative of the financial and economic concerns of Canada today, anyone aware of the assumptions which went into the creation of the budget, will recognize that current money supply is certainly inadequate to meet the government's cash requirements for the 1982-83 fiscal year.
There is, Mr. Speaker, an old song we would all recognize which extols the virtue of the west. One of the lines in that song is "Where seldom is heard a discouraging word". Well, I can guarantee, Mr. Speaker, that that no longer applies today in western Canada, eastern Canada, northern and central Canada. Discouraging words are the words of the day. Words of pessimism, disillusionment, unbelief and anger are the kinds of words you hear spoken throughout our country when it comes to discussing, describing and explaining the economic programs of the Liberal government.
I have just returned from four days in my riding, a riding which is famous for its rather frontier-like mentality. By that I mean an atmosphere of enthusiasm, optimism, faith in the future by people who assume that next year will be better than this year, that the lives of their children will be better than their own lives. It is a real and built-in sense of optimism which has prevailed in our part of Canada for many, many years. However, Mr. Speaker, that atmosphere of optimism and hope in the future has been thoroughly dashed by the
February 16, 1982

policies of this government, particularly the November 12 budget.
During the last four days, Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity to meet with a number of young people in my riding. I want to tell you it was very disappointing to talk with them and hear that they plan to drop out of school, that they see little hope in continuing their formal education because people they see with advanced degrees and professional and technical training are unemployed, and there appears to be little room for optimism over future employment. These people are despondent and thoroughly fed up with the kind of economic and political leadership coming from their leaders throughout the country.
I talked with senior citizens also, Mr. Speaker, and the central theme of their gatherings is people discussing and describing today's conditions as they relate to their memories of the 1930s, that in fact these are depression years. They talk about the eventuality of soup lines, about the loss of farms and homes, the kind of discussion they recall from their youth.
I have spoken with miners, loggers and cattlemen. A level of frustration exists in their area of the country which is quite different from other parts of the country. These people are directly attached to the resources of Canada, the grasslands, the mines and the forests, and they know what potential exists in those resources. The mills are closing, the mines are closing, and the cattlemen are unable to make any decent return from their grassland operations. This has resulted in an incredible level of frustration, anger and bitterness directed at governments and political leaders generally.
1 spoke with women and heard their tales of woe concerning their attempts to keep their families from falling apart, how they worked to keep some semblance of a home and family life when the main breadwinner had been thrown out of work, and when their children were disillusioned with their school studies. Women have attempted to assist the economics of their family operation by attempting to find work but have been unable to do so.
Again, the level of family strain was reflected in a report this morning in The Globe and Mail concerning the city of Kamloops. The report described the unbelievable situation concerning crime rates. In the major population centre of Kamloops, the crime rate is now twice the provincial average. Sexual offences have jumped by 71.8 per cent over last year. Weapons offences jumped by 71.4 per cent over last year. Robberies were up in excess of 10 per cent. The local RCMP detachment, which blames the economy for the increase in robberies, solved only about one in four of the more than 10,000 crimes in a city of less than 70,000 folks. The mayor blamed the economic stresses of the Kamloops area for the increase in sexual and violent offences. Again, this kind of straining of the social fabric of Canadian society is a direct result of the economic conditions in which we find ourselves today.

If one meets with the officials in human resources and the CEICD offices, they will outline the difficulties they face while trying to provide for people qualified for unemployment insurance. They are experiencing backlogs of hundreds and hundreds of cases. People are forced to go to the welfare offices when, in fact, they ought to be receiving cheques from the UIC. A strain is placed on the provincial coffers as a result of federal inaction and inactivity. When one speaks with small-business men, one finds that there is no longer any discussion of expansion of small business. There is no more discussion with regard to hiring and moving into new areas or attempts at new entrepreneurial activities. It is really a matter of survival, just hanging on and praying that those interest rates will be dropping in the next few weeks or months. However, these businessmen know full well, from what they read or hear in the media, that interest rates are likely to go even higher in the forthcoming months.
These are direct human responses to the economic challenges and problems facing us. I suppose another aspect which is becoming more interesting all the time is the underground economy, as people work to do an end run around the traditional economy and move away from the recording of transactions into a cash society, again to avoid the tax man and to avoid being part of the regular economy.
Why do people want to avoid paying taxes? Why is it that most popular bestsellers in the bookstores at this time of the year outline ways and means to beat tax men and avoid paying taxes? The reason is that the people of Canada have lost faith in what the government is doing. They have lost faith that the $6.6 billion which is being requested here today will be well spent in the best interest of Canadians. They feel it will be spent in the best interests of a select group of Canadians.

I noticed with interest that the Tory finance critic said that we must pray. God knows, we must pray. He said we must pray that Ronald Reagan is successful because, if not, we will have a tough time selling our policies to Canadians. You bet he will, and they will. They will have a tough time selling Reaganomics to Canadians at the rate they are going in the United States. That is an appropriate term-"at the rate they are going in the United States". Most financial analysts and economists are now predicting that interest rates this summer could be as high as 25 per cent in the United States. With the trends that we see across the way and from our colleagues to our right, our rates will be closer to 30 per cent if that is the case.
It is all right to say that we must hang in on those particular policies. That is okay for some folks, but what about the 1.8 million people who are not working today? What about the hundreds of thousands of people on fixed incomes? Are they able to ride out another two or three years of this policy as we experiment with people's lives to see if this economic policy works?
Our monetary policy has been in place in Canada since 1976. It has been in place because we wanted to bring down the rate of inflation. I ask anyone in this House, has the rate of inflation come down during that period? As interest rates have gone up, so has inflation. Surely we are not prepared to continue with this mindless approach to solving our economic problems, as the Liberals suggest we ought and as the Tories suggest we ought to accelerate.
We have a long way to go. Perhaps the best indication of the serious problems facing us when it comes to investor or consumer confidence is that people know the government is not spending their tax dollars wisely. How do they know? They know that from reading the Auditor General's report for the period ending March 31, 1981. The Auditor General makes a number of interesting comments. Let me quote just a few. He said:
In my view, the accounting policies which the government follows result in a significant overstatement of reported assets and understatement of reported liabilities.
That is why we say that the deficit is increasing. While at this moment we are asking for authority to borrow $6.6 billion, because of this statement we know full well that that figure will be much higher. The Auditor General went on to say:
-since many government activities are carried out by organizational entities which are not "departments", significant assets, liabilities, revenues and expenditures are excluded from the financial statements.

What are the objectives of this government? What are its objectives in terms of spending $6.6 billion? We heard the other day that the government felt it was in the best interests of the taxpayers of Canada and the Canadian economy to invest $100 million in a copper mine in Peru. The 1,500 people in the copper industry who have been laid off will find that hard to understand.

Up to 4,000 when you consider the auxiliary areas. It is hard to understand in my own riding, the copper centre of Canada. We have hundreds of people unemployed. There are hiring freezes in all the mines. A number of small mines are looking toward government support to enable them to open their operations. They find that $100 million at 11 per cent is going to help the Peruvians. It is hard to understand the logic behind that; indeed, there probably is no logic at all.
The one area where we in the NDP differ from the other parties is that we have some viable solutions. I want to talk about the most fundamental solution to our economic crisis today. We have heard a great deal about the need for increased confidence in the economy, that we must send a clear signal out to our domestic capital markets as well as foreign markets that Canada is a good place in which to invest. At the moment that is about as far from the truth as it could possibly be. Who has confidence in the next ten years in our country, or even in the next ten weeks? There is so much indecision, instability, unknown factors, a continuously changing economic climate as a result of government policy, that no one is particularly interested in investing in the future of this country right now. Why should anyone be with the returns one can get on their money from Canada Savings Bonds or simply from putting their money in short and long-term deposits? Why take a risk? Why take a chance when you can be guaranteed returns of 15 per cent and 20 per cent?

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
speechtext: How about 1916 per cent from the government?

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
Or 19'/2 per cent from the government, as the hon. member indicates. Why take a risk when you can simply put your money into a secure situation and collect that kind of return?
Taxation
We can be confident that there are solutions and that we can act very quickly. I ask hon. members to consider for a moment that when our country finds itself in a state of war, in a matter of hours we bring into effect a whole set of contingency plans. Things begin to happen overnight. I suggest it is time to declare war on the economic crisis facing this country, and move accordingly.
Something we must do before all else is to clearly map out an economic or industrial statement, strategy or blueprint for our country which has the co-operation of not only the federal government, but of all provincial governments, local governments, industry and labour.
As we sit here today, it is relatively clear in our own minds what that particular economic and industrial strategy ought to include. It must include three key factors. It must include what I like to call a key input industry sector, those industries supplying input into key sectors of our economy. There are three-housing, transportation and food. I choose those three sectors because that is where between 80 and 85 per cent of investment goes-food, housing and transportation. If we were to identify those three critical sectors as sectors where government investment will be taking place alongside private investment, it would send a clear signal out for all people interested in investing in the future of Canada.
My friends to the right claim that we in the NDP are interested in spending money, always taking money and throwing it away. I would like to challenge that. What we are advocating is not a need to spend money but to invest it. There is certainly a difference. We might class $100 million to Peru as spending money, but $100 million invested in the food industry of Canada would be a financial investment, not financial spending. It is not a matter of additional dollars but a reallocation of funds. The money is there now, being used in rather peculiar ways. What we advocate is that that money be reallocated into areas where we are bound to receive a productive return.
A second proposal in terms of a comprehensive economic strategy would be the strengthening of basic "building block" industries. Many are located outside the country, but these industries supply inputs to other industries which supply final products. I refer to the chemical industry, the creation of telecommunications equipment, the creation of industrial machinery and equipment, the forest industry, mining and small-scale power generation. We in the New Democratic Party are not convinced that the economic future of Canada depends on megaprojects. The best investment in our energy future is not necessarily a massive influx of both private and public funds into megaprojects at this point. Putting all our eggs into that one basket in these particular times is taking a great risk indeed. With these "building block" industries we could move into a third area; Canadians would be able to specialize and develop export-oriented industries.
We in this country have a number of strategic economic advantages other countries do not have. We can identify areas

February 16, 1982
Taxation
in the energy sector. We can identify areas in the resource sector. We have financial ability. We have human expertise. There is a number of areas in which Canadians have a natural strategic advantage in terms of developing specialized products which serve not only our domestic market but also markets around the world. We have seen that we can compete in a number of areas. Telecommunications is one of the obvious ones. Transportation is another one. Canadians have been world leaders in relation to both rail and aircraft. With a very clearly articulated strategy which would have the support of industry, labour and the three levels of government, I suspect that would send a clear signal out to investors both within Canada and beyond that this is the place to invest money and that such investment would result in long-term and stable returns.
At the same time we could begin talking about reduced interest rates. The fear of many people is that by reducing interest rates, let us say to one point above the inflation rate, the result would be a mass hemorrhage of capital out of our country. Why is there not a mass hemorrhage of capital out of Japan? Why would anybody invest in Japan where interest rates are in the 6 per cent to 8 per cent range, when they can invest in Canada with our interest rates being what they are?

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
speechtext: Because their inflation rate is 2 per cent to 4 per cent.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
One of the reasons, of course, is that when we invest in major manufacturing enterprises in Canada and when we invest in our resources sector, we are investing our money not for two weeks or two years, but for 20 years or 50 years into the future. I say that interest rates are simply one factor in that decision-making process. If we in our country can provide an atmosphere of confidence, if we can provide very clear signals that we have a very well thought out and clearly defined and credible industrial strategy, and if we reduce interest rates to one point above the rate of inflation, I suspect investors will be falling all over themselves to get into Canada, knowing full well the returns they can expect.
There is a need for research and development; that is well known to all of us in this House. Why is it that research and development is not going on at the moment? Is it because Canadians are ill equipped to carry on adequate research and development through to production? In many cases we are because many of our best minds are leaving the country, but I suspect that the real and fundamental reason research and development through to production does not occur in Canada is because we have more foreign ownership here than any other western industrialized nation. Why would a branch plant want to conduct research and development in competition with other plants of its mother company or with the mother company itself? If a person wanted to invest in research and development and could put his funds into his head office in Japan or a branch plant in Canada, where could that research and development be expected to take place? Obviously it would not take place in the branch plant. There is no incentive
to do research and development in the branch plant. That plant is there to serve a small market.
As the previous speaker said, we lack the incentive to get out and market our resources and the goods we manufacture. Again I ask why a branch plant would want to market its goods aggressively in competition with its own mother company. As long as Canada maintains its international reputation as a country with more foreign ownership than any other western industrialized nation there will be little incentive for research and development. There will be little incentive to open up new markets for our manufactured products.
Therein, of course, lies a challenge to us. We need to patriate more of our economy, but not along the lines of the national energy policy and the move into the oil industry. The theory is good, but what is happening is impractical. I suspect that the national energy policy is ill conceived.
With a clearly thought out economic strategy and a monetary policy to complement it there would be no need for discussions on foreign control and no need for additional government spending, because government spending would be focused in such a way as to make some sense. I will use the example of tourism in our country. There could be tourist activity in almost every corner of the country. A message should go out to the private sector that the federal government, in co-operation with provincial and local governments, feels that tourism is a priority and a key element in our industrial strategy. The private sector would respond if the federal government were to redirect and reallocate funds to tourism.
At the moment the situation is rather pitiful. We should be reallocating existing funds to tourism. The federal government should do its share, perhaps by way of international marketing or providing low-interest loans to certain kinds of entrepreneurial activities. The provinces should be co-operating within that same framework. All ten provinces plus the territories should agree that if the federal government is going to provide leadership in the development of tourism, they will complement that activity and develop infrastructures-in ski areas, for example. The provinces and territories should assist in the development of beachfront marinas and so forth. Local and regional governments could also participate in this same context. They should agree to participate and assist in developing the necessary infrastructures. Then the private sector would come in with the construction of hotels, ski lodges and whatever. With that kind of co-operation and economic leadership coming from all three levels of government, we could provide a creative environment. The clear message that would be sent out to Canadian and perhaps foreign entrepreneurs would result in a very sophisticated tourist industry of which we could all be very proud.
We should apply the same policy to a number of other sectors, particularly where Canada has some strategic edge in terms of national and international competition. That is the kind of solution we in the New Democratic Party recommend for consideration. When we have our discussion in the Committee of the Whole, I hope the Minister of State for Finance will take into consideration the option I have just laid out.
February 16, 1982

That is the kind of thing that the federal government should be developing at the moment rather than simply following, in a mindless way, certainly not a very independent way, with the support of its Tory colleagues, the policies of Mr. Reagan in the United States.
