Mr. Speaker, this is a bill that attempts to deal with three totally different measures. It is an omnibus bill and, despite the ruling of Madam Speaker earlier today, 1 must say in disgust that it is difficult to debate a bill that deals with three principal problems, three types of taxation-borrowing being a form of taxation I suppose-all in one package. I shall attempt to deal first of all with the borrowing authority, then with the excise tax bill and then with the amendments to the Income Tax Act.
If you or I went to our bank or credit union and said we wanted to borrow money, Mr. Speaker, I suspect the manager would ask how we propose to repay it. Yet the minister has come to this House of Commons for the third time this session asking to borrow money, with no plan to pay it back. He came to the House with Bill C-30 and asked for $12 billion; he came to the House with Bill C-59 and asked for $14 billion-and he got it; and today he comes with Bill C-93 and asks for $6.6 billion. That is a total of $32.6 billion in less than two years, and he expects us to give it to him.
It is a disgrace that a government elected in February, 1980, now less than two years into its mandate, should come to the House of Commons to ask for a total of $32.6 billion. Did it tell the people of Canada that when it promised honest, decent, straightforward government? Did it say to the people of Canada that within two years it could be coming to the House of Commons demanding to borrow $32.6 billion? Yet that is what it is doing.
The government brought in a budget which it said was based on equity, restraint and renewal.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
speechtext: Equity for whom?

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
speechtext:
The hon. member asks, equity for whom? For those who make more than $53,000 per year, the tax rate is reduced to a maximum rate of 50 per cent. For the 54 per cent of the people earning $30,000 or less per year, the tax rate is increased. That is Liberal equity!
And what about renewal? Sixty-two members of this party travelled across Canada holding public hearings on the question of renewal. They did not find a single business, business organization, social service agency, trade union or group of any kind anywhere that was prepared to say it was optimistic about Canada, that it would build in Canada or create in Canada because it was enthused about the renewal offered in this budget. The way this government uses the word, "renewal" means renewal of expense, bigger government, more state interference. That is the kind of renewal this government offers. There is nothing to stir the people up, nothing to stir the soul or make people get up and build a country.
Taxation
I am reminded of what happened in this House of Commons 110 years ago today when a bill was introduced to finance the greatest megaproject this country has ever seen. I refer to the bill to finance the Canadian Pacific Railway. At that time there was a government that had enthusiasm, that was prepared to lead, to offer projects that would build a nation from sea to sea. Today we have a government prepared to ask for another $6.6 billion to put us further into the red, to figure out another move to tax oil and gas wealth-and I shall talk about that later-with its Henry VIII type of tax system. We have a government that has no sense of renewal, no sense of building Canada, no sense of the worth of Canadians. All it does is create an ivory tower for itself.
And what about restraint, Mr. Speaker? In December, 1979, a budget was introduced in this House which indicated in its projections for the year 1981-82 that the Government of Canada would spend, on a national accounts basis, $66.2 billion and would tax from Canadians in the same fiscal year $59.6 billion.
Let us look at the restraint proposed by this government which now asks us for more money. Let us look at what in fact is happening due to the totally inept management of the economy of Canada and the waste and throw-away programs of the government.
The government this year will spend $76.6 billion; this government this year will tax $69.2 billion. But the government of the Right Hon. Joe Clark, the government that had the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) as its minister of finance, would have spent in total $66.2 billion. If we had MacEachen for fund raising and Crosbie for spending, we would not need to borrow any money; we would have a surplus of $3 billion. Instead, what do we have? We have a deficit that gets larger and larger and carries on without any effort being made at restraint at all. The government asks for another $6.6 billion, and if we look at the records we know that it could have a surplus of $3 billion if it exercised the type of restraint that was evident in the budget planning process of two years ago. There is absolutely no reason that this House, at any time, should consider this type of bill.
When you or I go to our banker to borrow money, we normally show need, Mr. Speaker. I decided to look, as we all should every week, at where the money is in Canada. The Government of Canada has on deposit with the chartered banks of Canada $6,947 billion at the present time. The minister can see that in the Bank of Canada statement of February 11, issued last Thursday. The Government of Canada has on deposit with the chartered banks right now nearly $7 billion.
Does the government need to borrow money? The minister said that the spending requirements for the year will be only $6.6 billion. The government has all the money it needs on deposit with chartered banks. What more money does it need? Why does it need more money when it has that kind of money available right now? Let me point out that when the Govern-

February 16, 1982
Taxation
ment of Canada deposits money with chartered banks, it receives on the amount of over $100 million a rate of interest 10 per cent less than the rate of 90 day treasury bills.
The Government of Canada was prepared to pay people 19.5 per cent on Canada Savings Bonds. The same government is prepared to lend money to the banks at 13.4 per cent this week. The government has $7 billion with the banks on which it is prepared to make 13.4 per cent, yet the minister who is supposed to be in charge of financial institutions comes into the House of Commons and says, "I need to borrow $6.6 billion". He does not need to borrow it at all; he has it on deposit at 13.4 per cent. What a travesty, what an error!
This reminds me of the errors in the budget-there have been 25 changes so far, and there are many more to come. Is a $600 million mistake when dealing with the provinces a minor one? The bill is for $6.6 billion, yet the government has nearly $7 billion on deposit in the banks at the same time.
I should like to look at the rationale for giving this government this money. Last year the government came to the House seeking $14 billion. It said it wanted some elbow room or freedom. Out of the $14 billion it still has borrowing authority for $3.9 billion, so it has lots of freedom within which to borrow. It wanted elbow room, so we gave the government more money than it could conceivably need. What did it do? It went out on the market last September and offered Canada Savings Bonds at 19.5 per cent. At the time the government made that offer, all indicators showed that interest rates were dropping rapidly, yet it held the 19.5 per cent offer open for people to lend money to the Government of Canada until November 6. On November 6 it could have borrowed all the money it required, including the cost of borrowing, for approximately 16 per cent. However, this government, which is supposedly careful with our money, entered into a borrowing arrangement to borrow, as the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) indicated, on-demand money at 19.5 per cent. My calculation of the cost of borrowing that money, including the commissions paid for one year, is 20.5 per cent.
In reorganizing its loan, the government increased interest rates on all outstanding Canada Savings Bonds to 19.5 percent, for a real cost of about 20 per cent. It could have borrowed the money on November 6 for 16 per cent. It cost the Government of Canada, and therefore the people of Canada, 4 per cent extra on $25 billion for a year. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres), the man who is in charge of financial institutions, cost Canadian taxpayers $1 billion in that move alone. Now the Minister of Finance is called, "The billion dollar man". Should we give these people the freedom of financial movement in order to borrow $6.6 billion, when the history of their borrowing is such that they are totally irresponsible in their use of the borrowing authority and paid $1 billion more in interest for a $25 billion debt than should have been paid? It is unconscionable to ask the House to support this portion of the bill.
Let me turn to some of the figures. When the government took power on February 18, 1980, for the fiscal year ending
March 31, 1980, the total amount paid in interest on the Government of Canada debt was $8.6 billion. This year the "glorious" Minister of Finance is saying that the cost of carrying our debt will be $14.7 billion. Did Liberal members promise Canadians during the last election campaign that the result of their inept management would be to increase interest charges in two years by $6.1 billion per year? Is that what they promised? Do Canadians recognize what they have in terms of inept, stupid and incompetent management? Also the minister went on to say that the interest costs will be $16.5 billion next year and nearly $18 billion the following year. Did he tell Canadians in the February, 1980, election campaign that the country owed $67 billion in that year and that we would owe $92 billion as of February 1 ? Did he tell Canadians that it would cost them borrowings of $25 billion in two years to support the government? Did he tell them that this was restraint and that it was in the budget program of the government?
The government comes to the House of Commons, and we are really its bankers, because we allow it to borrow money on the credit of Canada. When Liberal members sought office, did they tell their bankers that they would run the debt up by $25 billion in two years? There is no justification for this bill.
I should like to deal briefly with the interest rate policy of the government. Actually it is not an interest rate policy. I have difficulty in even suggesting that it is a policy. It is really a mishmash of effort. We all remember when the Governor of the Bank of Canada said that he would allow an increase in the M-l, that is the monetary targets, to be between 4 per cent and 8 per cent. In order to keep up the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar last year, they cut down the increase in the money supply so that, in fact, it was negative. Of course we wondered why there were huge interest rate increases. The reason was that investment confidence was driven out and hot money at the highest rates the country has ever paid was imported. They passed on that cost in order to keep the exchange rate high and, to ensure that it worked, they deferred our monetary policy to an exchange rate policy.
It is not a government of tight money; it is a government of no money for anyone. It is a government which operates with short-term palliatives, which has no sense of where it is going, which struggles from pillar to post, which has driven out longterm markets for financing so that they no longer exist. It is a government that says interest rates shall be determined every Thursday by some sort of phony auction of Government of Canada treasury bills. It is a government that makes sure there is no long-term money in its budget provisions; a government that destroys one of the few long-term sources that are built into our system, namely, the insurance and annuity industry. With the budget the government makes sure that the insurance and annuity industry will be robbed of a long-term investment cash flow of $1.75 billion this year alone. How much more will it be the following year?
February 16, 1982

It is almost impossible, if not quite impossible, for a person to obtain a five-year mortgage. The kind of loans people get today are those that bear an interest rate that can be changed on three days' notice. We wonder why there is no confidence in the system. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the minister have both said that this is to counter inflation. Let me tell you, Sir, there is no countering of inflation with this kind of monetary policy. This is not a high interest policy. This is no policy. This is a policy of pillar to post. This is a policy of Thursday interest rates. This is a policy where there is no confidence in the supply of money at all.
We do not know what the rate will be this week. It may be higher, it may be lower. We do not know what it will be next week. It depends on what is going on in the United States. Maybe it will be higher or maybe it will be lower. In any event, there is no confidence.
How can a person invest, build a plant, buy equipment and create productivity in the country? I see the minister responsible for housing standing up. I ask, how can a person build or buy a house? You have to be an idiot to buy a house in this market because you cannot get a mortgage for any length of time. If you do, you play Russian roulette. Think of a young couple who buy a house with an 18 per cent mortgage on it. They think they can pay that mortgage, but they do not know what the mortgage rate will be in August when it comes due. Will that mortgage rate be 22 per cent, 30 per cent or 35 per cent? Who would have thought ten years ago that the government would pay 19.5 per cent for the money it borrows itself? Who would have thought that the rates at Household Finance a short time ago would become today's prime rate at the bank?
People have no sense of confidence in the monetary direction of the country. Does this bill give us that? Does this borrowing authority? Does the government's financial policy do the things that are supposed to be done under the financial policy of the government and does it come to grips with this problem? Not at all. The government leaves the unmistakable impression that it does not know where it is going.
Last Saturday 1 listened to a young Greek lad speak to a policy panel hearing. He dispassionately and rationally talked about what had happened to the Canadian dream. He is a young economist. He mentioned the inflation caused by the Vietnam war, the changes that happened as a result of OPEC and the international problems with the United States essentially losing track of the cost of gold. Then he talked about Canada. He said that, instead of coming to grips with these international problems, we were making things worse; deliberately making things worse. We were not taking advantage of our resources. We were not taking advantage of the entrepreneurial nature of our people. Indeed, we were driving out business. We were turning away ideas. We were preventing research and development. With our budget, our fiscal policy and our interest rate policy, we were making sure that the country would be less successful than it would otherwise be. Without the government at all, we would be better off. The
Taxation
policies of this government make things worse. That is what we must address.
He mentioned that one of the major causes of our problems was the National Energy Program. Part of the national energy policy is in this bill we have before us. It is a bill in connection with the Excise Tax Act to increase the taxes on natural gas. The minister says that the bill has something to do with an agreement between the federal government and the government of Alberta.
This bill ought to have something to do with fairness, with honesty and with where we are going. That is where the problem comes with the bill. The bill sets out the tax rates on natural gas to January 31, 1982. The bill then goes on to create a new paragraph 25.19 (a) through to (e). In order to figure out what happens, you have to turn over to page 8 of the bill. The bill sets out what can be charged per gigajoule for gas, per cubic metre of methane, per cubic metre of propane and per cubic metre of butane. All of a sudden you see what we are getting into with this bill. Whereas the rate for natural gas was 63 cents a gigajoule, there is now the authority to increase the tax on natural gas from 63 cents to $4. Next we come to ethane. We get the authority to increase the tax from $11.65 to $75 a cubic metre. When we get to propane, we get the authority to increase the tax to $105 per cubic metre from $16. For butane we can increase the tax to $115 a cubic metre from $17.85. This is a Machiavellian type of section. It establishes the limits to which the minister can increase the taxes. This is the first time in my experience that I have ever seen a tax law which says that taxes can be anything up to a certain limit that the minister by order would like to make them. That is what it says. The taxes can be anything up to a limit that the minister wants to order them.
For example, the price of ethane goes up a possible total of 543 per cent. In other words, the minister can put his hand in his pocket at any time and say, "I have decided today that ethane is worth more tax and I can increase the taxes 100 per cent, 200 per cent, 300 per cent or whatever I feel like and not come back to Parliament."
Now, how can we as members of the House vote for a bill which would conceivably allow the Minister of Finance to levy any tax he wants up to a maximum level. We have a tax right now where the rate is 63 cents per gigajoule, or $16 per cubic metre, or $17.85 per cubic metre, and then all of a sudden it can be increased, in the case of pipeline gas, to $4 a gigajoule; in the case of ethane, to $75 a cubic metre from $11.65; in the case of propane, from $16 a cubic metre to $105. This can be done without reference to the House. The minister may increase the tax by order in council.
Now, Sir, if King John at Runnymede had proposed that type of arrangement to the barons, I suspect the same thing would have happened to him as happened to Charlie. I suspect, Sir, that even if Henry V111 had suggested this type of tax arrangement to Parliament, the strongest of the Tudors would have lost his throne. However, we have a government which

February 16, 1982
Taxation
comes in the name of Parliament and democracy and says that we should authorize the government at any time to increase the tax on a product such as ethane by 543 per cent, or 556 per cent for propane, 544 per cent for butane and 534 per cent for natural gas. How can we as Members of Parliament vote for that bill? It does not really matter whether you are a Liberal or a New Democrat. No matter what you are, how can you as a Member of Parliament vote for a bill which would enable a minister of the Crown to increase taxes by ministerial order in any amount and at any time he wants to? Now I want to leave that part of the act for a moment and go to that part which deals with the PGRT.
That, Sir, is probably the most complicated piece of statute work that 1 have seen for some time. Clearly, it is the type of thing that must drive business right out of the country. We talk about encouraging people to come to explore for gas and oil and that type of thing, but we wind up with the most convoluted and complicated clause of a bill that one has ever seen in Clause 3. We wind up with terms such as "incremental oil revenue", "incremental payouts", "incremental production royalties", "incremental resource royalty". I do not know what an incremental royalty is on incremental production. Presumably "incremental" applies to old oil. I do not know. Sir, whether you have ever seen a jar of old oil and a jar of new oil to determine if there is any difference. Old oil is oil which comes from fields discovered some time ago, or even fields which have not been drilled but were discovered prior to the first of this year.
Now if you drill in those fields and get oil, then you pay the 16 per cent PGRT tax on everything you take out, subject to certain deductions for Crown royalties. In addition to that, if there is any incremental revenue-in other words, the price is higher than it used to be-then you pay 50 per cent of whatever that is. In the name of whatever is holy, there must be some method by which the law officers of the Crown can simplify the law or do something, because this tax, in its computation and application, is so complicated that it can only be of benefit to the accounting profession and those who come from Philadelphia and practise law.

It sure does. The last thing I want to talk about in the time remaining is the criticism which has been hurled across the floor, all too often: What would you do? Well, in our 1979 budget we clearly set out what we would be doing. We clearly set out where we could restrain government expenditures, and we declared-this is on the public record- that we would have spent no more than $66.2 billion this year.
What would we have done? Well, we would not have got into the mess in the first place, and we would now be working our way out of it. We would be cutting back on the overhead of government. They say, where is that overhead? Well, the Auditor General talked about a measly thing like the $50 million spent on excess photocopy costs. We have the minister of propaganda over there and he spends a $100 million.
However, there is a whole host of other things. We know that in our offices, we know it when we go down to the photocopying room, we know it when we order paper around here. We as Members of Parliament know what goes on just in the House, that these things are nice but do they have to be there? We know it when we go to government offices and see a series of people there reading novels, when we do not hear a typewriter going. I have pointed this out to ministers, 1 have told them that I have been to their offices and did not hear the sound of a typewriter in a half hour while in the waiting room. There is a lot of fat in this government. There are a lot of things we are doing that could be cut back. That is the first thing we would do.
Second, we would turn the budget around 180 degrees. Instead of discouraging business and driving it out of the country as they have done-at least six times as much money left Canada on average last year as did throughout the 1970s-we would be bringing it back in. We would be giving businessmen something to cheer about, something to get enthusiastic about. We would be operating like the government of Sir John A. Macdonald did 110 years ago when he said to Canada that we can grow, we can build and become a nation from sea to sea. That is how we would operate, with enthusiasm, encouragement, with less government and more trust in Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have the opportunity to contribute to the debate this evening because the second reading of Bill C-93 gives me an opportunity to voice my very strong opposition to the economic policies being pursued by the government. I believe it is the same overwhelming opposition expressed by Canadians everywhere, by farmers, small and large businesses, home owners, consumers, economists, opposition parties and, yes, even some government members and Members of Parliament; yet the government continues to hold fast to its position, content to remain unaware of what is going on around it in the real world.
February 16, 1982

What we have before us is legislation which would further implement a budget which is in no one's interests or continued economic wellbeing and, quite rightly, is opposed by just everyone, as I mentioned earlier, including some members of the federal cabinet. For this reason, this bill to borrow $6.6 billion of taxpayers' money is very hard to accept.
We must ask, what does the government intend to do with this money? Will it raise money to help those Canadians who need help, such as our farmers, our small businesses, our home owners, the poor, the elderly and the unemployed? No, in this budget there is very little evidence of substantive relief being offered to those Canadians who need it most.
We hear constant talk from the government about tight money supply and that we must continue to tough it out regardless of what happens. If things get worse, and surely with the government's economic policies they will, the minister says, "So be it, because sooner or later we will hopefully be better off'. This promise is not good enough for us. Flow long do we have to wait? How long do Canadians have to swallow the same old story and continue to watch their economic livelihood and their future fall to pieces?
Mir. McDermid: 1984, election year!

One would think that after seven or eight years of miscalculated economic and monetarist policies, and a policy of deliberately high interest rates, that the government would finally get the message that its policies are just not working and that they will not work in the future. Everyone except the government is in agreement with this point.
All this talk of economic restraint and belt tightening would be easier to accept if the government practised what it preached. While it increases its spending by 22 per cent, increases the deficit and raises taxes, all in the name of restraint, it is quite willing to punish those Canadians who spend, who wish to invest or take risks or save for the future. This, to me, is a double standard. In other words, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is saying, "Do not do as I do; do as I say, and we will all be better off for it". This is really nonsense. What we do have before us is an economic policy which is a blueprint for recession. As if this were not enough, we have a government which is deliberately bringing the economy to a complete halt. It is deliberately creating a recession. I believe the government is prepared to create such a recession and create unemployment, and it has deliberately raised interest rates in pursuit of an absurd and nonsensical policy. At the very least, if the Minister of Finance is going to stick to this ruinous economic policy, he should be prepared to help those Canadians now who are suffering the most from those policies.

The government has failed to keep its election promises to lower interest rates, to wrestle inflation to the ground, to fight unemployment, to ensure cheap energy prices, to lower the budget deficit and to help Canadians suffering from economic hardship. The government has completely failed to even address these problems. When we are asked to look at a bill which seeks to borrow over $6 billion-

-we have an obligation to look at the government's over-all economic policies.
It is very clear that the Minister of Finance did not look closely at the policies he introduced on November 12 because on a number of occasions since then he has either withdrawn or revised several measures, realizing the mistakes and miscalculations he tried to push on Canadians. How many changes does it take for the minister to realize the budget is a complete failure?
In spite of what the government may say both inside and outside the House, the November 12 budget introduced a major increase in personal taxation. Canadians can expect no less than an average $1,400 federal tax increase in energy costs per family, such as the increased taxes on gasoline and home heating fuels, for each year over the next five years.
We also have a massive increase in federal spending. Government spending is going up by 22 per cent this year while the deficit will remain at $13 billion, higher than the figures forecast by the government.
Not only will Canadians feel the bite of higher taxes in the energy field, but through a series of underhanded tax changes, Canadians will be taxed on many employment benefits such as private health care and dental plans, daycare, the use of car and travel passes, as well as the immediate taxation on retirement allowance, all in the name of closing tax loopholes.
The insatiable drive for more revenue also extends to life insurance policies and registered retirement savings plans. In the case of RRSPs, Canadians can no longer deduct the interest on loans taken out to buy into the plan, meaning there will be a major drop in savings for retirement, not to mention investment initiatives in the economy.
Tax changes toward annuity contracts and life insurance policies strike at the very heart of the principle of encouraging Canadians to work toward their retirement income and life insurance protection. If this provision is retained, it will put Canada in the embarrassing position of being the only industrialized country that taxes life insurance.
For some strange reason the government seems opposed to the principle of Canadians planning and providing for retirement. This development should concern Canadians all the

February 16, 1982
Taxation
more because the federal government's own pension plan, the Canada Pension Plan, is in very deep financial trouble.
There are other areas of the federal government's economic policies which have created massive opposition and severe crticism. I am speaking here of the Small Business Development Bond. The government boasts that it has extended the bond program to unincorporated farmers and small-business men. However, the rule changes made this assistance less than what farmers and small-business men had hoped for or what they clearly need.
The bond has been completely emasculated and does not really resemble the previous Small Business Development Bond program before the presentation of the budget. This program has, quite simply, been switched from a development bond to a survival bond, intended only for businesses in desperate financial difficulties. No farmer or small-business man who wants to expand his operation will get a Small Business Development Bond. In fact, he is not eligible for a bond unless and until he is on the verge of bankruptcy.
There is no question that those who face immediate foreclosure need help and need it now, but what about those businesses that are in a position to expand operations and create badly needed jobs? Should they not be encouraged and helped? Not so, says the Minister of Finance. They have been left out in the cold to fend for themselves.
As if these changes were not enough to cause frustration and anguish, it has become clear from what many constituents have said that the banks which administer the Small Business Development Bond are reluctant to process applications because there is considerable confusion on the part of the banks and the government over how the new bond works.
The Minister of Finance has given very little evidence of his willingness to help in solving this problem. A more active intervention here is essential in order to make sure that those who need assistance receive that assistance now. Otherwise we will see more farms and businesses fade into oblivion.
Quite a number of my constituents have expressed to me problems they have encountered with their farm credit applications. While the government has introduced legislation which offers badly needed but very limited financial aid, applications continue in some cases to be processed too slowly. This is very distressing, given the fact that many farmers are in need of immediate financial relief but are going under because of these delays.
The bankruptcy figures speak for themselves. The government's high interest rate policy is driving an ever-growing number of farms and businesses into foreclosure. In the first 11 months of 1981, some 7,261 businesses were forced to close their doors for good, while 258 farming bankruptcies occurred during the same period, an increase of 133 per cent over the first nine months of 1979.
One sector of the farming industry that is particularly hard hit is the beef producer. Rising production costs, increased machinery prices, higher interest rates and depressed beef
prices have all combined to force this industry into a depression with very little hope of recovery in the foreseeable future.
With well over 1.2 million Canadians out of work, coupled with thousands of bankruptcies, common sense should indicate that the federal government would see the light and take concrete and positive action to alleviate these hardships. However, the government insists beyond all reason that the road to economic recovery lies in a tight monetary policy so as to bring down inflation and interest rates. But, as I said earlier, this policy simply has not worked. Inflation is over 12 per cent, unemployment continues to rise and interest rates are on their way up again.
On the matter of unemployment, the Minister of Finance refuses to listen to the calls of some of his own cabinet colleagues who ask that the government stimulate the economy and create new jobs. No substantive programs have been announced to help our unemployed.
There is no question the government's economic policies have to be changed to reflect our national and pressing concerns. The budget is already out of date. It was written last fall and placed on the shelf gathering dust until the debate on the constitutional resolution was over. By the Minister of Finance's own admission both inside and outside the House, the figures used are out of date and are therefore inaccurate and misleading.
In conclusion, I urge the Minister of Finance to introduce a new economic policy that more accurately reflects the current economic problems we are now experiencing. Without substantive changes, Canadians will be faced with a detailed blueprint for a depression, a depression as devastating as anything we have seen since the 1930s. I do not think that even this government would like to see that.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to speak on Bill C-93, an act to amend the statute law relating to certain taxes and to provide other authority for raising funds. This bill combines the more conventional borrowing authority bill with a number of other amendments to the Excise Tax Act arising out of the November 12, 1981, budget, and amendments to the petroleum and gas revenue tax which implement the Ways and Means motion to amend the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on January 7, 1982. In looking at the bill, I find approximately three pages on the borrowing authority and approximately 30 pages on the rest. This indicates that perhaps the government is trying to sneak something by us. Perhaps this is in keeping with the way this government operates.
Until about five years ago, borrowing bills were introduced mainly as part of supply. Five years ago it was decided that borrowing bills would be introduced separately. Now we find that included in this borrowing bill are two other amendments to acts. I have looked through the bill, and I cannot find one single link between the borrowing part of the bill and the
February 16, 1982

amendments to the Excise Tax Act and the PGRT Act. I wonder why the government decided to include those provisions and borrowing authority in the same bill at the same time.
I will deal just briefly with the Excise Tax Act and the PGRT and finally with the borrowing provision in the bill. An excise tax is a tax on a specific commodity, and in this case the commodity involved is energy, oil and gas. The federal government has agreed with the provinces that it will not tax exported natural gas, but that is only in relation to natural gas taken from provincial lands. The federal government retains the right to tax exports of gas taken from federal lands. I wonder why the federal government wishes to retain that right.
The Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act was implemented by a ways and means motion on January 27, 1982, and one wonders what connection that act has with borrowing authority. The PGRT is basically a tax to increase revenues to the federal government. By this tax the federal government will take in approximately $23.1 billion over the next five years. With that amount of additional revenue coming in, 1 wonder why the federal government will need to borrow.
By the excise tax alone the government could raise up to $8 billion a year. This bill would raise the tax on natural gas per gigajoule from 57 cents to 63 cents, but the bill provides for a limit of $4. If the government were to increase the tax to the limit of $4, it could raise up to $8 billion a year. The government will not have to come back to Parliament if it wishes to increase this tax over the years.
One wonders whether the government is attempting to sneak some of the provisions in this bill by the House. I understand they will be debated in the Committee of the Whole and not in a standing committee. This means we will be able to question the minister, but we will not be able to call witnesses. We could do that only if the bill were to go to a standing committee.
The three pages of this bill dealing with borrowing authority would provide the government with the authority to raise $6.6 billion in Canadian or foreign funds. As I said in my last speech on a borrowing authority bill, I wonder why the government is interested in borrowing in foreign funds.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very happy to entertain a question at the end of my speech.
The article in The Globe and Mail went on as follows:
The demand figure has dropped primarily because of continuing high interest rates-many consumers have been frozen out of the market because they simply cannot afford houses at current interest rates.
The article goes on to say that the figure of 177,000 housing starts registered in 1981 was inflated by the MURB program which was rushed to completion at the end of 1981. It states that HUDAC expects huge rent increases because a number of rental projects were built under the federal government's Assisted Rental Program, and that half of them had mortgages in the 10 per cent to 11 per cent range which will now go to the 17 per cent to 18 per cent range.
The bad news continues, Mr. Speaker. HUDAC also predicts that the provisions of the recent federal budget will exert upward pressure on rents. The president has stated that rent increases of up to 60 per cent will be common on many of these units. The article states that the low number of housing starts will add substantially to Canada's high unemployment rate. This is contrary to what the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) has stated in the House.
One has to ask why the government needs to borrow $6,6 billion. It has $7 billion in the chartered banks and it has $1 billion in the Bank of Canada. Why does it need $6.6 billion now? Does it have some patronage to look after? We are told that patronage by the Liberal Party amounts to over $2 billion per year-a figure that the Liberals refuse to confirm!
Does the government have some secret loans to cover? Just recently in the House a member asked a question about a loan being made by the Export Development Corporation to Al-
February 16, 1982

geria for a tower structure which will contain a restaurant and an observation deck. The middle floor will contain many things, including film clips-I expect even a clip of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dancing when he was in Algeria last fall. This loan of $47.25 million will cover 85 per cent of the total construction costs.
It is impossible to get any information on this loan, however. The government will not state the rate of interest, the term of the loan, or the term of repayment. The Export Development Corporation states that Algeria has an unlimited line of credit. In other words, it will not tell us how much money it can lend to Algeria but has stated that if Algeria came to the corporation tomorrow for an additional loan, the government would automatically give it.
That is the type of loan the government is giving out to other countries when there are hundreds of thousands of people without adequate housing in this country, people who cannot renew their mortgages, yet we are prepared to lend $47.25 million to a socialist nation.
What does the Auditor General think of the spending of the national government? In his report dated March 31, 1981, he stated:
The national debt now stands at $82.8 billion. Servicing the debt in fiscal year 1980-1981 cost more than the total of all corporate income taxes collected. It accounts for more than one-fifth of every tax dollar, and its load burdens all the people of Canada like a huge, high interest mortgage.
It is an albatross around the necks of Canadians. Sometimes it is difficult to put this matter into perspective-and I will return to the Auditor General in a moment-but let us look at a situation wherein average Canadians, without taxes and without the payment of various benefits, could perhaps live on $20,000 per year. I use this as an example only, but when Canadians start paying income taxes, taxes on highways and medical benefits, something different happens. If we look at the latest report of the Economic Council of Canada, we find that out of every dollar spent in Canada all forms of government spend 50 cents. If individual Canadians could live on $20,000 without any benefits and then give half of it to government, we assume that they could still live comfortably because the government would be providing other benefits.
Chapter 9 of the Auditor General's annual report dated March 31, 1979, contained perhaps the most serious evidence of inadequate management of human resources from the standpoint of economy and efficiency by reporting the results of performance measurement tests in levels 1 to 4 of the clerical and regulatory occupational groups which consist of some 50,000 employees across government. The test concluded that government employees operate at 60 per cent efficiency. Thus, to return to my point, if average individuals could live on $10,000 per year and the government collected $10,000 per year, we assume that individuals would be receiving $10,000 in benefits, but in actual fact the Auditor General may be correct when he assumed that we are only receiving 60 per cent efficiency out of the $10,000. This means that we are paying $10,000 to governments to provide certain benefits, and we are

only receiving $6,000 in the way of benefits. In effect, 20 per cent of the $20,000 to which I referred is being wasted. It is another example of government inefficiency.
If one looks at government revenues and expenditures, one finds where the money is going and what is happening. One finds that government revenues are 16 per cent less than its expenditures. As the Auditor General stated, the government is not spending money efficiently. This is something to which we must address ourselves over the next number of years. Why do Canadians have to live with high interest rates? The Minister of Finance rose in his place time and again to say that it was due to inflation and that we must reduce inflation. As I have stated previously in the House, there has been a massive outflow of long-term capital over the last two years. If one examines the national accounts balance, one finds there has been an outflow of $17 billion in long-term capital in the last two years. During the same period there has been an inflow of $16 billion in short-term capital, money which will remain in Canada for a period of anywhere from 30 days to one year. In the investment business it is commonly known as hot money. Hot money moves around, based on high interest rates. If our rates are higher than those of other countries, it will flow in; if our rates are lower, it will flow out. In effect the government is hiding the true reasons. It has created conditions whereby investment in Canada has been discouraged and the outflow of capital has been encouraged.
What can the government do? It could encourage investment in the country. The United States was built upon foreign capital, yet it controls its resources at the present time. Canada is a young country and needs foreign capital. Government officials travelling abroad have to defend it and say that Canada really wants foreign capital, but when they come to the House of Commons they fall in behind the government line which says that we want to control our own destiny and to nationalize all energy companies. What else could the government do? It could allow the dollar to float.
The Minister of Finance stated that a decline in the dollar would be inflationary. What does he think high interest rates are if not inflationary? In 1976 the government brought in the current policies, and the Bank of Canada carried them out. The government could reduce interest rates by 3 to 4 percentage points, which we on this side of the House have recommended. The government could encourage the export of various commodities such as natural gas. The province of Alberta estimates that it could export surplus gas of up to $2 billion per year. This would help the western provinces; but since the government does not presently have any seats west of Manitoba-and in the next election it will have none west of Ontario-it decided that it did not want to help western Canada.
At present the Bank of Canada holds approximately 20 million ounces of gold valued at $8 billion. Some of that gold could be sold off to provide support for our dollar. Certainly the situation is not hopeless. One must ask how many more firms must go bankrupt before the government comes to its

senses, or how many more farms must fail before the government wakes up.
We do not need a budget that contains a multitude of economic tax changes. We need a budget that is a blueprint for the future, not a maze. There are many fiscal and monetary measures that take time to implement. A decrease in the deficit takes time. While the dollar could decline, it will not decline immediately, it will decline slowly if we implement some of the measures we suggest. There will be a higher cost for imported goods. Everyone understands that. But in addition to that, there will be an increased amount of exports, which would be of benefit to Canadian manufacturing firms. That is understood by many Canadians. Why the Liberals do not understand it, I will never know. It takes time to reduce inflation. We understand that, but we must start to do something. There are things we can do immediately, such as providing a real housing program. The housing program we have now provides nothing.
We need 100,000 rental units next year. The government is providing help for 15,000. We have over 1.2 million people who will be renewing their mortgages over the next two years, and the government is going to help fewer than 50,000 of them; that is very little help. If the government were to provide real incentives for housing we would see higher employment, therefore lower unemployment. The president of HUDAC stated today that because of government policies there will be a loss of jobs this year to the tune of 90,000. That is an astounding figure, and it is shocking that we have to live with higher unemployment in the coming year.
An opinion has been put forth by the government, supported by the NDP, that the banks are responsible for these high interest rates. Let us see who makes the high interest policies. From where do they come? Your interest rates and my interest rates are decided by five people. These five people are the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, two directors of the Bank of Canada and the deputy minister of finance. From where do all these decisions come? They come from the other side of the House. Those are the people who implement these high interest rates.
As we look to the future, the next couple of years do not look very prosperous for Canadians. This government has brought forward a budget that does not help ordinary Canadians. If government has brought forward a borrowing policy of $6.6 billion, and we do not know what it is going to do. If government comes forward with two other pieces of legislation in the bill. Why are these two pieces of legislation joined together when there is no link? Obviously there is something the matter with what the government is presenting. I would be surprised if any legal mind in government employ could find a legal link between these pieces of legislation before us now.
In conclusion, we in the Conservative Party would like to hold out some hope for people that life will not be all downhill. But what we see coming from policies across the floor are higher interest rates, higher unemployment, no growth, more
bankruptcies and more farm failures. In the short term it looks like disaster. But we hope at the next election people will decide that they have had enough of this Liberal government.

Tonight I want to talk about the borrowing authority bill before the House. First I should outline some specific things, which this particular legislation, along with the entire government's financial policy, has meant to people in my riding. They reflect the millions of other Canadians who are not faring well under the present government's economic strategy.
February 16, 1982

Since February, 1980, we have seen that problems have increased in this country. Unemployment has become more severe. People have lost homes because they can no longer handle high interest rates. The compounded effect of taxation and increased energy rates are wreaking hardship on people. Everything culminated in November when the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) presented a budget. The budget relates to borrowing authority. Unfortunately, the budget did not in any way address the real economic needs in this country.
I have had the pleasure of sitting in this Flouse during the time when two other budgets were presented. 1 felt there were some positive things in those budgets. The over-all thrust of these budgets were criticized, but nevertheless there were items that showed recognition of the problems and suggestions were put forward to address the problems. The last budget of 1981 completely failed to address the needs of Canadians. I think that view is a unanimous one across Canada. 1 suspect the government acknowledged its failings when it presented the transitional measures. Members of the government caucus recognized the failing when they start writing letters to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) advocating that some real measures to help Canadians be taken. It is interesting that the government can continue on a tack of self-destruction.
When I look back to the Thirtieth Parliament and what was happening in my area of the country, and I am sure it was happening everywhere, I note that the government thought that the answers to the economic problems of the people of Canada at that time were wage and price controls. Of course, that translated directly into wage controls. That program led to absolute chaos and reduced labour relations to a terrible state. It turned an enormous number of people against the government, and I am surprised-I guess I should not be surprised after watching this happen so many times-that a government could continue the mistakes of the past when everyone in the House, certainly on this side and perhaps some members on the other side, realizes what the outcome of those failed policies is going to be.
Another aspect of this bill is that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) feels that he can grind more out of the working people of this country with these absolutely ridiculous proposals to tax these benefits which are designed to induce people to move to remote areas in order to harvest our natural resources. A complete disaster, Mr. Speaker, for which they will eventually pay the price at the polls.
Looking at their high interest rate policy for a moment- and I will deal with this in more detail later-I Find that there are many cases in my riding of individuals who are faced with losing everything they have ever worked for. I know members on that side are receiving mail identical to mine, and I do not understand why there is not more from the backbenches of the government to the effect that we have had enough, it is time we changed the policy. However, for the time being, believe me, they are getting this mail because we are getting copies of
Taxation
it and it is harmful. Those people are experiencing the same problems we are.
But we come tonight, Mr. Speaker, to the borrowing authority and again we find a consistent theme. I am not sure, along with many others, where we are headed. Possibly during this debate we will hear members on the other side come up with some idea of where they think we might be headed. I see the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) is in the House, and perhaps that is as good a place to start as any. He is of course well aware of the events taking place in the Comox-Powell River riding and other areas of British Columbia and, I understand, other areas of Canada. Something like 60 per cent of the forest industry is unemployed in that area. As a result, we have a situation where there has been a tremendous demand on unemployment insurance. The Fishing industry has been saddled with tremendously complex regulations and punitive and discriminatory measures taken against Fishermen in those regulations. The end result is that there are enormous claims and the ofFices are not able to deliver unemployment insurance. Because people are required in some cases to wait three to four months for unemployment insurance, the burden has shifted. These individuals have been laid off, their income and savings are gone, they have nothing with which to pay rent, and many of them have nothing with which to buy food. In the end they apply for social assistance. In British Columbia unemployment insurance offices were telling people, "We cannot help you. It will be two to three months before your UIC claim can be processed. Go to the welfare office".
So, Mr. Speaker, essentially what happened is that this minister and his department were incapable of developing a program which the House felt was necessary, and the burden fell squarely on the province of British Columbia to deliver welfare. Unfortunately that burden in those offices was so great that to get a hardship cheque to put food on the table was taking three weeks. I had a man appear at a meeting in Campbell River who said he had not eaten for two days. His wife was in the hospital in Nanaimo and he had to leave his kids with a friend in Port Hardy because, as he said, he was down here in Campbell River sitting on the doorstep of the welfare ofFice to get a cheque to feed his kids. He said, "I have never been out of work before and never collected unemployment insurance".
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to having a chance to evaluate this government's performance by going to the polling stations, you know where he is going to be, and there are people like that in many of the ridings of the members opposite. It is time they did something. However, it is not just the unemployment insurance program. There are many other programs on which we will have to get cracking to see that they have adequate funds for staff resources, proper training, and distribution of those resources so they can serve the people of this country.
Returning to the subject of fishermen, the fishing industry in my riding is one of the basic resources and basic sources of employment. Many of the fishermen have worked at this all

their lives; that is the only thing they know. Some are well on their way to the point where they will never be able to work at another task because fishing is all they have ever done. And because of what I would suggest is incompetent management of the fisheries resource, we would have to go back to the plan put in place by Jack Davis as they key to it. They felt they were doing people a favour by reducing overcapitalization of that fleet. In fact, they turned around and created a capitalization nightmare where it cost an enormous amount of money to buy licences. Those were, of course, financed on the assumption that interest rates would not rise beyond all reason. Those people, because of openings and closings and the strategies of the Department of Fisheries were forced to upgrade their equipment; bigger boats, faster motors, greater capacity. Essentially, they had to borrow money to enhance the capability of their vessels. More capitalization, more borrowing in order to stay in an industry that was being managed in a very poor and inefficient manner.
Having done that, the government then decided it was time to jack up fuel costs. Some of those vessels run 400 or 500 miles along the coast of B.C., they are very fuel intensive, if you will, and the cost of that fuel has risen significantly. Their return grows smaller and smaller each year. Then we have the real kicker, namely, interest rates. So what happened, of course, when the market for fish turned down, is that many of the fishermen were faced with foreclosures. The bankers appeared on their doorsteps and said, "We are going to have to foreclose on your vessel". The fishermen knew the banks were not going to get anywhere with that program because no one would buy a fishing vessel off the coast of British Columbia today. If you cannot fish, what is the point of having a high price boat? What the banks could do is to take away their opportunity to earn a living, and many of them are at a point in their lives when they have no other options.
So the banks said, "We will not take away your method of earning a living and we will not foreclose on you if you will put your house up as collateral". Now they have their house and fishing boat. Some of them went so far as to say, "Give us a co-signer, too, a friend with collateral behind you". And the fishermen, in order to stay in business, did it. Well now, there sits the bank with the government's high interest rate policy, with the home, the fishing vessel and the assets of friends and relatives on the line. In fact, the banks have now started to foreclose because the bank has an opportunity to retrieve their investment. People are now losing everything they have ever worked for, their fishing vessels, their homes, and friends and relatives are being badgered to pay outstanding debts. The consequences of that, Mr. Speaker, are going to be very serious. If it keeps on being as bad as it is, I think they will be asking for more than serious consequences at the polling stations.
If there is any doubt, I would suggest that any hon. member opposite, or the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc), should pick up the phone to call any bailiff who would say what they are doing, straight out. An interesting
thing is that many fishermen did not have a good season this year. These fishermen went down to the unemployment office, but the regulations for obtaining unemployment insurance are so complex that one almost needs to be a Philadelphia lawyer to interpret the UIC regulations for fishermen. However, these fishermen are waiting three or four months for unemployment insurance benefits. Many have been put on welfare and many are having great difficulties by being forced into this position. The consequences are extremely serious. A very important resource is being poorly managed and a group of people are being very poorly treated. It is time that the government put up a fund so that these people can be at least protected from losing everything for which they have ever worked. This should be done, whether the government does it through the minister responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission, through the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans or the Minister of Finance.
I would like to speak for a few moments only about some of the things that this borrowing authority, putting aside government spending, could do for Indian communities. In my riding there are 18 basic Indian communities. Again, they face problems much like any of the others. I would select maybe two bands from the coastal Indians as examples to illustrate what the government could be doing instead of what it is doing right now.
It is my understanding that the government has developed an envelope system. The word is that the government has put $26 million into a social affairs envelope and has tried to hold the line on costs. At the other end of the process there is an Indian band at Bella Coola which draws a budget together at the beginning of the year. The band said it needs $1.8 million to run the band, and they are not fooling. That is their basic bottom line cost. That provides basic necessities for people on social assistance, because the government policy is not designed to help Indians create economic development or to put people in those communities to work. That is basically the amount of money required to hold them at the subsistence level. Many bands are budgeting at that level. However, the band at Bella Coola included provision for some economic development and housing development, and they arrived at a budget of $1.8 million. As this budget filtered through the system with no consultation and no real consideration, it joined the district budget in Vancouver with 51 other bands. It then joined the B.C. region, went to Ottawa, and Ottawa said it would chop $25 million off the region, just "bang". "Make it do", is what Ottawa said. When it came back to British Columbia, it went to the region, and the regional manager was stuck with accepting a budget which was $25 million short, and trying to feed people, build houses for them, and provide education for their children. It must keep the regional manager awake every night of the week to try to figure out how he will do that while dealing with human lives and misery. However, then it went down to Bella Coola, and the regional manager and the district manager eventually said to the chief and the 500 people who live at Bella Coola in the band and in the village, "You have to get by with $1.3 million".
February 16, 1982

What will happen? Most of their population is under 18 years of age, and they will be forming families in the next few years, and the demand for housing will simply skyrocket. Their children have never graduated from high school. It has been a terrible situation. The education system is not acceptable. They have developed a band school, but there is no funding for it. They cannot meet the payroll for the teachers. The teachers will leave and the kids will lose this year.
However, there is another interesting matter for the minister responsible for unemployment insurance. It might pay if he were to take a look into this matter tomorrow morning. In Bella Coola there are many people with pending unemployment insurance claims. The band was counting on the fact that it would not have to pay welfare to those people who did work. However, there are unemployment insurance claims which have been pending for three or four months. This band is roughly 300 miles up the coast of B.C., and those people had to be paid welfare until their UIC claims were processed or until the band ran out of money. Right now, the band can no longer pay welfare, and its budget was to last until the end of the fiscal year. Now they cannot meet the payroll of band officers, and they can no longer pay schoolteachers to educate their children. They cannot even pay welfare to the people who are unemployed. Those people have no income, and in some cases there is nothing left to eat. Part of this situation has been caused by pending unemployment insurance, a matter which could be resolved if someone would pay some attention to that community. Basically, budget costs cannot be cut off at that level.
1 know that this borrowing authority is down from last year, and the Minister of Finance is expecting to get pats on the back. But, believe me, if he would get his butt up to Bella Coola and have a look at the reality of what those kinds of cuts are doing to people, then, by gosh, maybe we would have a different kind of borrowing authority before us.
Yes, when you get stuck in the ivory tower here, I think the world appears much different from the reality. Fishermen are now faced with losing everything for which they ever worked. Indian bands in Bella Coola are attempting to pay real, basic costs with money which does not exist. Senior citizens and handicapped people in those communities have the same problems as we do. However, they are told that they will receive $6,500 for all of those support services. If some of those ministers over there would go into those communities, they would come out without their hair, and that is the reality, and I would be there to help them.

not only true of my riding. Certainly constituents of other hon. members are dependent on the forestry industry. The forestry industry is in a very serious situation. We see a lot of money being produced in a lot of other areas to help out. We are finding that funds are being put up for work-sharing programs, and they are being directed to various communities. However, what we need is a strategy in areas like the one I represent, which will be of assistance to those communities. There is no possibility of work sharing when the mill is shut down and when lumber can no longer be exported.
However, there are other alternatives. The forest industry has upgraded the resource for years. We have carved trees out of river valleys, and now the trees are a long way up in the mountains and are extremely expensive to harvest. There have been fire burns, and disease has ripped through the forests. In those areas, there is a tremendous need for reforestation, and new jobs could certainly be created which would protect and enhance that resource for future generations. If we were to move seriously in that direction, some of the current dislocation in the forest industry could be currently offset by jobs created by federal-provincial co-operation in intensive reforestation and forest management programs.
There are options which are not being considered. This borrowing authority could include funds to provide for those kinds of projects. This would have an immediate impact on small business and communities in those areas.
I would like to indicate briefly how some of the small businesses are fairing in those communities because of the shutdown in the forest industry and because of the inability of fishermen to bring revenue into the communities. The other day, 1 had an interesting telephone call from an individual, a small-business man, who was attempting to collect overdue debts in one of those communities. His accounts receivable had risen to the point where his cash flow was very seriously affected. To his surprise, the small-business man found out, by phoning around to 20 businesses which owed him money, that none of those businesses were in a position to pay him. As a matter of fact, many of them said, "Forget it. I doubt if I will ever be able to pay you back a nickel because I am facing bankruptcy or receivership. My creditors are on top of me, and I cannot collect my accounts."
This malaise, this disease or disorder, has spread right through the entire economy. It is extremely important that the government become realistic and not fall back on economic theories, I guess, which have been gleaned from the nineteenth century or even earlier. We have been told time and time again that the cure of the disease arising from high interest rates will be certainly far worse than anything we ever expected.
The question of fiscal restraint in the government being applied now is complete foolishness. In some cases the government could create a stimulus or an investment in the community which frees and moves other dollars. The kind of government restraint now in place will not do anything except harm people further. We are back to the old suicide configuration.

In those remarks, I hope, I have put forward a positive suggestion or two, or a direction which the government may take that could help many of the individuals and specific groups being harmed.
There is one other area I would like to touch on in the short time remaining. It affects both coasts of this country and the industrialized areas of central Canada. I refer to the whole marine industry. It appears we are looking forward to a period of time in which offshore resources and the development of resources on Canada lands will lead to an enormous potential in the marine industries of Canada, shipbuilding and allied trades.
The Royal Bank of Canada, in its estimate of expenditures between now and the year 2000, states that resource development investment might go as much as a trillion dollars. We had billions projected in the megaprojects task force report. There is general consensus that the amount of money available for Canadian industry, if we plan properly, is enormous. In the marine sector in particular, the building of offshore platforms, supply ships, the infrastructure, the communities, the dredging, there is an enormous amount of money available to Canadian industry and an enormous job potential.
We talked of this for many months when Bill C-48 was before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. At one point, two ministers, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) appeared before the committee. They said they understood the problem, and that, as far as the law goes, they wanted us to leave it totally in their hands. They said they would take care of the problem because they recognized it. In a very candid way at a closed meeting, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce suggested he had it well in hand with a committee of roughly 24 people, which he called the committee of industrial benefits. They were going to capture for Canadians the benefits of our offshore development.
The reality is that it is going to be a colossal failure. Time after time he was in the House when the matter of the ships being built offshore was raised. They are being built in Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Europe and the United States. He agreed they were being built there, but asked us to look at what else the government has done. He was often proud to mention the Burrard drydock in which the government invested so heavily. Unfortunately, the drydock was built in Japan. He mentioned that the same had been done for Dome Petroleum. Of course, some of their vessels are being built in Japan.
A very different view of what Canadians were going to be able to do was given by the oil companies when they appeared before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. They stated that, in reality, Canadians are not ready. They want to move quickly. They have a need for
equipment and specialized personnel. They told us that, quite frankly, unless we moved yesterday, we are not going to be able to capture the benefits we would expect.
In Britain and Norway, roughly half a million jobs came out of the development of offshore oil. Half of those jobs were created in the United States. Another quarter were created in the industrial parts of Great Britain. The parts of the country in which the industrial activity or resource activity should have occurred were those areas which had been depressed for years, yet we found that very few jobs were created there.
Now we are looking at development off Atlantic Canada. Within a few years we will probably be looking at it off British Columbia. I say to the government that British Columbians and people in Atlantic Canada are looking for the benefits to accrue to this country. We want our shipbuilding industry to hire Canadians, not import help from offshore. We want those jobs to accrue in our yards. Frankly, this will not be done with 24 people in an industrial benefits office. The British used thousands of people. They used enormous numbers of engineers for evaluation and development of those programs. By the time the project had reached full speed, the British had managed to capture a large number of those jobs. Unfortunately, we do not show any inclination to do that.
In terms of government involvement, borrowing authority and economic programs, this is discouraging more Canadian involvement in our Canadian industry and opportunities for Canadian employment than we are getting. I believe that at the present time the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has created more jobs in the marine industries in Europe, Japan, the Far East and the United States than he has in Canada with the programs he has in place.
There are many other areas in which that particular sector has been held down and depressed for years. My colleagues from the province of Quebec must express concern about the development of the shipbuilding industry in that province because it is an important one. However, it also affects Ontario, the maritimes and the west coast of this country.
For years we have said it is time this country got going on developing its own merchant fleet. We ship offshore enormous amounts of grain. We let the Chinese, Russians, Americans and Europeans haul it away. We do not carry the product.
The United Nations put forward proposals that 40 per cent of a nation's goods should be carried in its own ships. It would give a stable base for that operation. For years we have not seen a move on that. The government has fought it right, left and centre.
A few months ago, during the Grey Cup game, the Canadian Pacific Company, our old friends which have been intimately involved in hauling our goods in and out of the country, placed an ad on television. It showed the Beaverford, an old CP vessel which was an armed cargo ship during World War II. It conveyed goods back and forth across the Atlantic. I believe the Beaverford had two very small guns. That ship was attacked by a German pocket battleship. It managed to hold the German ship for five and a half hours while the rest of the
February 16, 1982

convoy managed to escape. It was a miraculous feat. It was hit by a torpedo and all hands were lost.
Unfortunately, CP capitalized on that. It said this was their tradition in the past, fighting for Canadians. They were trying to link that tradition with their tradition of today. Their tradition today is to have their ships registered in foreign countries. They moved from Bermuda. 1 guess they were not getting a good enough deal there. They moved their ship registry to Britain and Hong Kong. They sail their ships with foreign crews. Frankly, neither I nor my children are interested in the future that CP has for this country until those ships are registered in this country, are sailed by Canadians, and the returns from those efforts come back to Canada.
