Mr. Speaker, in dealing with Bill C-93, I wish to deal with Part I, the borrowing authority provision, which grants the government the authority to borrow some $6.6 billion.
Rather than dealing with the various economic theories and putting blame on the government for the record high inflation

February 16, 1982
Taxation
it caused, the record high interest rates it has caused, the record high government borrowing it has made necessary, the record high government budgetary deficits, the record high government spending, the record high unemployment and record number of bankruptcies, I would like to direct my thrust this evening to the plight of a segment of our society which usually does not get much attention from the House, yet it is the very foundation of our present society and, most certainly, the society of Canada in the future. I am speaking, of course, of the family unit.
As we are all too well aware, the family has had to endure enormous strains in the recent past, and this has brought about extensive changes to its structure. Some are for the better but, unfortunately, a great many of these changes are to its detriment. The changes are continuing, and no one can predict when the situation will stabilize.
The stresses of today stem from many causes, but one prevalent result is family breakdown. There has been an alarming increase in the number of divorces in Canada-a 70 per cent increase, in fact, since 1970-with no sign of a reversal of this trend. The number of single parent families in Canada has been growing, to the point that 10 per cent of all our families are now headed by one parent. Our statisticians tell us it is more than likely that that parent will be a woman, since the heads of eight of ten single parent families of every 100 will be mothers.
In the years between 1969 and 1973, there were close to
150,000	children involved in divorce actions, and the number affected has been rising yearly. These children will most likely be living with their mothers and this, far too often, means living in poverty and, frequently, on welfare.
Although a single father has some of the same problems as his female counterpart, he is not nearly as likely to be subjected to her most serious concern, that of poverty.
Poverty does not present just one problem, but many. The quality of life in general is affected by poverty. Some of those undesirable qualities are instability, alcoholism, mental strain and low educational achievement.
Since poverty is often at the root of these social ills, the lone woman parent is in a precarious position. Facing a heavy load of responsibility, she must continuously bear the pressures of child rearing and, as was pointed out, too often in poverty. These women run the overwhelmingly high risk of being poor.
Statistics show that nearly half of the mothers living alone with their children will find themselves existing below the poverty line, and nearly all of the half-a whopping 98 per cent-on welfare.
Along with the grinding poverty of welfare goes the feeling of inadequacy and the stigma of isolation and discrimination. Certainly this is not the emotional environment that fosters the self-reliant and stable kind of future citizens we want to see our children become.
The reasons for the economic deprivation of such a large proportion of households headed by women are many, and all levels of government and society must share the blame.
Efforts to provide income security and needed services in Canada have involved different kinds of legislation; some exclusively federal, some exclusively provincial and some cost-shared by the two levels of government.
Under the Canada Assistance Plan, the federal government shares costs with the provinces of social services provided by the provinces to persons in need. This includes mother's allowance, child welfare maintenance, health care services for the needy and the extension of welfare services in many other general areas.
However, the constitutional division of responsibilities has resulted in this "patchwork quilt" system. This system has succeeded in binding many of the poor, single women so tightly with bureaucratic red tape-with rules and regulations that are counterproductive-that they soon give up hope of ever becoming self-sufficient, contributing members of society.
Since our present economic climate almost necessitates that both parents work outside the home and since it takes two to keep the family solvent, the single mother and her children fare very poorly in such an environment. If she tries to find employment, she discovers that women's wages are considerably lower than men's. In fact, her pay will likely be 50 per cent less than a man's, and she will have little opportunity to upgrade her skills.
The most serious problem facing the single mother who wants to enter the work force-and indeed the major headache for all working parents-is to secure adequate care for children during the hours they are away from the home. The need for substitute child care has increased dramatically, but this need has definitely not been well met at any level.
Practically 90 per cent of working mothers must seek private arrangements for their children's care. These alternatives to a regulated centre have been documented in the book, "The Kin Trade", written by Laura Johnson and Janice Dineen. They say child care conditions in unsupervised homes are often profiteering and unsanitary, and that there is an epidemic of child neglect and widespread abuse. The care substitutes are too often grossly incapable of giving the children adequate care at its most basic levels, let alone any kind of stimulation or nurture which will enrich them.
There are 600,000 children under the age of seven who have no access to daycare. In the few areas where there is excellent daycare, it is available only to the very rich who can afford it, or to the poor whose fees are subsidized. All our children are entitled to the very best possible care that we can give them.
What of the centres that do exist? They are subject to few legal standards to ensure that enough staff is hired or that they have been properly trained and are adequately paid or that the physical environment conditions are suitable for children. We licence and supervise many things in our society. Our hospitals and restaurants come under severe and constant surveillance for the maintenance of sanitary and safety standards. The physical surroundings of our children who must be away from
February 16, 1982

their own homes for many of their waking hours does not seem to matter very much.
We are told by experts in the Field of human development that the first few years of life are so crucial, so vital, that the whole of a person's future social development, self-esteem and ability to cope and contribute to society depends on that initial nurturing.
Let us ask ourselves what value we place on that fact. It is as important to our children-perhaps even more important to them-that they have adequate care as it is for them to have an adequate education.
We worship at the knee of higher education, yet ignore the very rock upon which the learning capability of a person is established, the early childhood experience.
Can you see something wrong, something very wrong with our priorities when we give our colleges and universities millions of support dollars and then dole out an absolute pittance to the care facilities of our youngest citizens?
How can we rationalize the monetary-value priority we place on university professors compared to that granted to early childhood educators who themselves must live on the brink of poverty?
Free education through high school is extended to every Canadian, and yet the very crumbs of our money, our interest, our concern and our support, go toward the initial step in the education for living. 1 contend, Mr. Speaker, that our emphasis is wrong. Not that secondary education is not important, but of what value is it if the students have been neglected in their formative years, with the resulting damage to personality and learning ability?
With the present high cost of child rearing, it is unrealistic to expect parents to manage the full financial responsibility of raising the next generation. To those with the mentality that says, "If they want children, let the parents pay for them", let me say that we need today's children and they are not to blame for having parents priced right out of their homes.
1 strongly suggest that this House pay serious attention to the national task force on daycare which has been recommending since April of 1980 that we pass a national daycare act.
This act would stipulate that provincial programs must have adequate child-staff ratios, adequate levels of staff competency and suitable physical environments before they can receive federal money, rather than being eligible for federal cost-sharing regardless of the standards of the daycare supplied.
The National Agenda for Action for Canada's Children, the report of the Canadian Commission for the International Year of the Child, states that the federal government has an important role to play both in directing more funds to the provinces for building and for the staffing of child care centres in order to improve the quality of those centres.
It recommends that federal funds be made available on a cost-shared basis for the construction and operation of nonprofit daycare centres meeting specified acceptable standards
Taxation
set by the provinces. National standards for the acceptance of the centres should be established too. Special grants should be made available to schools and other institutions wishing to adapt their facilities to provide for all-day care programs.
The report also recommends that federal subsidies be provided to the daycare agencies based on a sliding scale whereby the parent pays according to ability to pay.
It suggests also that the Income Tax Act be amended to provide tax incentives for all homes and institutions offering properly supervised, qualified, child care. The Income Tax Act could be amended to allow parents to deduct the full cost of child care up to $3,000 per child and taxable family allowances to be raised to the level suggested by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in 1970.
The Agenda for Action goes on to state the following:
At present, child care workers and other care-givers, are chronically underpaid. Child care is important work and those who care for children should be valued accordingly. In addition to the remuneration of care-givers-

speechtext:
In the event that I have any time left at the end of my speech, I will be happy to entertain a question.
The Agenda for Action continues:
-good child care is dependent upon well-developed programs and services provided by competent, trained personnel working under reasonable conditions.
The report recommends that child care should be available near the home or place of work and easily accessible to public transportation.
I should like to see tax concessions given to businesses and industries that provide on-site care facilities to the children of their employees.
Executives of businesses are beginning to realize that daycare is now a key management issue and is essential if women are to have equal opportunity in the work force.
As well as opportunity, women who must work are entitled to the least amount of physical and emotional strain possible in settling their children into their substitute home environment. At this point, I would like to congratulate several of the governmental departments which have made available such facilities for the children of their employees. May I add a word of personal commendation to Madam Speaker for providing such services for House of Commons employees. It is an enlightened step and one which I hope will be emulated by all government departments.
The wage-earning poor in Canada must be encouraged in every way possible to make it worth their while to work. If it is not, there will come a time when a top-heavy welfare class is going to topple our economic structures. Some serious thought has to go into tackling this problem head-on and some significant solutions must be found.

February 16, 1982
Taxation
The welfare mother who works part-time is allowed to keep a very moderate sum of her earnings above her welfare benefits. This is soon eaten up in babysitting costs and, as has just been pointed out, too often in an undesirable environment.
There are transportation and work-related expenses too. She is faced with discouragement every step of the way in trying to lift herself out of the welfare treadmill. Every effort must be made by governments, social agencies and society as a whole, to get her into the mainstream of life again, to be self-sufficient and self-respecting as a contributing individual.
Can there be any greater irony than the fact that a mother's care for her own child is considered to be of less value than that of a surrogate parent? At present, a welfare mother with one child, in Ontario, lives on about $5,000 a year, and yet a foster or group home is paid between almost $7,000 and $13,000 for the care of one child.
Being forced to stay on welfare and out of the work force is not only damaging to a single mother emotionally, but economically, to her and eventually to the country at large. If she cannot enter the work force until her children are older, she too will be older and will find it even more difficult to find productive and rewarding employment. Add to that the endangered position in which she will find herself during her later years if she has not had an opportunity to contribute to a pension plan.
Once again, the public will have to contribute directly to her maintenance. How much better for all concerned if she could have had the opportunity to provide for her later years herself.
There are few financial incentives to part-time employees and to low-wage earners. We realize that a great many of their number is made up of single parents, and the federal and provincial governments could assist them greatly by introducing practical income supplement programs.
A few provinces have taken some positive action in this area, and Saskatchewan is to be commended. Manitoba has begun a child-related income support program. Quebec's work income-supplement program, granting tax credits through the provincial income tax system, has the positive aim of encouraging low-income earners to remain in the labour force and to motivate welfare recipients who are employable to join the labour force.
I hope that consideration will be given by the House to the recommendations of the National Council on Welfare that the federal government set guidelines as a pre-condition for cost sharing, to bring about additional improvements to existing welfare conditions. It would require provincial governments to introduce programs in which there would be a reduction rate of family benefit payments, the rate at which benefits are reduced for earned income. Lone parents would be encouraged to undertake part-time work with such encouragement.
As well as in the work situation, there is another area where single mothers fare badly. When children remain with their mothers after divorce, as most do, it has been found that child
support payments are generally inadequate, non-existent or uncollectable. The Law Reform Commission of Canada estimated that 75 per cent of all maintenance orders are not enforced. This means dependants are often pushed back on the welfare rolls, and we know who foots the bill.
The legislation proposed by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) early last year would have dealt directly with this sort of situation. It would have given some much needed rights of enforcement to the courts, making maintenance and other money orders pursuant to the Divorce Act. It is regrettable that Bill C-250 did not receive more serious attention in the chamber.
The province of Manitoba would like to see a central federal registry of all maintenance and custody orders, with Ottawa expanding its role to cover enforcement of these orders. It wants an order issued in one province to be valid, coast to coast, and it calls for a federal-provincial information bank which would be of immeasurable assistance in tracing defaulting spouses. Manitoba has been the spearhead in insisting that family law receive its rightful attention in constitutional talks. Authorities of the province claim that if the divorce law is allowed to come under provincial jurisdiction, there will be ten different divorce laws. This would precipitate the danger of some provinces becoming divorce havens, and enforcement of court orders would be hopelessly tangled with ensuing costly litigation.
The whole area of divorce, separation laws, child custody, maintenance and alimony, needs a complete reorganization. We should give thoughtful consideration to laws governing these situations being federal and enforced by provincially-appointed judges, as is the system now used in the field of criminal law. I urge my fellow members to give their concerned attention to the matter of family law and to the best interests of all Canadians. Canadians should have the right, no matter where they live, to consistency and uniformity in this critical area. Between present federal and provincial avenues of control and legislative jurisdiction, the situation of the divided family has become a hopelessly snarled mess. It is the persons in these families with whom we are dealing, persons who have endured conflict and children whose homes have been broken because of conflict.
The most valuable national product of Canada is not gas or oil, not wheat or fish or minerals; it is the children of the country. Tragically those children and their wellbeing are not a priority as far as the Government of Canada is concerned. Our children are the most important asset we have in Canada. They will be making the decisions for Canada in the future and will be directing Canadian affairs. They need to be carefully nurtured and trained for their role as leaders of the country. They must be given every opportunity to develop into healthy, stable, educated persons with positive self-images. Unfortunately, because of the social upheaval of recent decades, not enough of our children are receiving such an upbringing or that kind of support, direction and encouragement. To our national shame, too many children are being neglected and deprived.

Mrs. Landon Pearson, vice-chairperson of the Canadian Commission on the International Year of the Child, made recommendations to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs in February, 1981. I should like to quote some of her remarks before the committee, as they were so relevant, urgent and vital to the present and future wellbeing of all children. She indicated:
-we can do a great deal better than we are doing with respect to our children. It is a question of priority. The potential is there.
Children will always end up at the bottom of the priority list unless they are a first responsibility to someone, and there is at this stage within the federal government no place where the child is a first responsibility.
She went on to say:
-children are a national responsibility as well as a national resource . .. and the responsibility for safeguarding and developing this resource is something which must be shared for it is a national, as well as a provincial, a community and an individual one.
In making their presentation, Mrs. Pearson and her commission members went on to suggest some recommendations to the federal government as to how best it could exercise its considerable responibility for the welfare of its youngest citizens who cannot speak for themselves. They were concerned about lack of co-ordination and the fragmentation of existing structures of programs at all levels of government which are concerned with children. They pointed out that there is no national focus or federal body which is exclusively responsible for the wellbeing of children.
The Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, upon studying the report, made recommendations which would further the basic goals of a strengthened family. This would help to create a climate of economic and emotional support for children, while promoting justice for them and defending their right to full development.
The committee was impressed with the need for the formation of a central mechanism to which the problems of children could be addressed in a continuing way. It saw a need for liaison among different levels of government and non-governmental organizations. This need would be best met by the formation of a specific structure for a secretariat for children's affairs, adequately funded at the federal level. Therefore it recommended that the government establish, within the mandate of the Minister of Justice and the Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Chretien), a secretariat for children's affairs, and it urged the implementation of these recommendations as soon as possible.
I congratulate the Canadian Commission on the International Year of the Child for its thoughtful and dedicated report to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. One third of our population is comprised of children, children who have no voice in their destiny, no vote, no clout, and whose interests are often ignored. We ignore them at our peril, for our future will be held in their hands, and we wish them as bright a future as we wish for all Canadians.

subtopic: MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-APPLICATION OF GRANTS IN LIEU OF TAXES PROGRAM
MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-APPLICATION OF GRANTS IN LIEU OF TAXES PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the questions to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) were asked some time ago, the whole question of grants in lieu of taxes must be in the minds of municipal taxpayers all across the country, especially in areas where there are concentrations of federal government departments and Crown corporations.
I put this matter down for debate tonight because in my own region of Ottawa Carleton which encompasses five municipalities and make up the constituency of Nepean-Carleton, the regional council is just now in the business of striking the

February 16, 1982
Adjournment Debate
regional rate which will impact on every taxpayer in the area whether that taxpayer is a home owner, a farmer, a commercial operator or an industrialist, if he either owns lands or rents property.
To the extent the federal government and Crown corporation properties are not valued for tax purposes in the same way as privately owned properties, the burden for providing municipal services in that area falls to a greater degree on the ordinary municipal taxpayer.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you have read the interesting submission to the federal-municipal grants task force by the city of Kanata in my constituency, supported by the city of Ottawa, wherein it was recognized that a problem exists because the federal government still has an arbitrary right to decide what is fair in its opinion in terms of grants in lieu of taxes. I want to read part of the brief. In part, the second paragraph reads:
Presently, where there are differences in the evaluation placed on federal property as determined by the provincial assessment commissioner and the federal government, the federal minister has the right to unilaterally decide on the evaluation. It is the position of the City of Kanata, as well as many other municipalities, that federal properties should be valued in the same way as those owned by private individuals. Hence it is essential that there be an appeal procedure whereby an impartial ruling can be made on the value to be used for grant purposes.
I think that is quite a reasonable proposition and I hope the parliamentary secretary will speak to that this evening.
The city of Kanata brief then touched on the difficult problem of business tax, particularly the fact that in that municipality AECL has said it is not bound to pay business tax, although it has made some transitional grants to assist. The city of Kanata took the position that there should be an impartial process to determine whether a Crown corporation is one that is to pay business tax or whether it is not one to pay business tax. This is also a reasonable proposition. Now it is done arbitrarily by government by order in council.
The city of Kanata also raised in its brief the position of Canada Post. In that connection we find the following:
One further concern is the way in which new Crown corporations will be allocated to a schedule. An example of this is the newly formed Canada Post. It is the city of Kanata's belief that Canada Post, under its new mandate, is the equivalent of a private business corporation. As a result it should be paying payments-in-lieu equivalent to both land, building, and business tax. It is understood that Canada Post has been placed in Schedule 3.
It is therefore not liable for business tax. The paragraph continues:
If this is the case then there should be some appeal process to determine whether or not that schedule is appropriate.
The proposal in this brief is one way of settling the difficulty that exists. I hope the government will listen to the importance of that.
While I am on the subject, and I have the floor with respect to the problems that affect us here in this area, I want to remind the parliamentary secretary of the immense relocation of government buildings to Hull, Quebec. No one will fault Hull, Quebec, for its good fortune, least of all me. But I want to remind the government of the presence in this area, particularly in the city of Kanata and in the western end of Nepean,
of the very important high technology industry in the national capital area. I want to say to the government that when it is considering decentralization of government departments or agencies, the importance of maintaining those government departments and agencies here in an area that can provide appropriate service to those government buildings and agencies should be considered.
I have one thing in mind, and that is a proposal to move the mapping surveys branch of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to Sherbrooke, Quebec. This is what a constituent of mine wrote to me concerning this. He said:
As a concerned citizen, and one who is very familiar with this government organization, I very honestly fail to comprehend just how anyone could make such a decision that might eventually cause the relocation from Ottawa to anywhere in Canada for such a high technology government branch.
As I am sure you know the surveys and mapping branch has the responsibility of producing maps and plans in varying scales for all sectors of Canada, and to carry out their duties they require very sophisticated equipment, in large quantities, in the disciplines of geodesy, photogrammetry and cartography with strong support from computers.
What I am saying, Sir, is that with respect to taxation there be some good reason for relocation. The appeal process proposed by the city of Kanata is a good way to find out really how much is owed both for business taxes and whether or not it is applicable, as well as grants in lieu of taxes. Secondly, I ask the government, when it is considering any relocation, to remind itself that in the city of Nepean and the city of Kanata there are land-use plans available crying out for government agencies, particularly those-although not limited to this- that relate to the high technology field. In those two areas there could be a great benefit to those two cities.

subtopic: MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-APPLICATION OF GRANTS IN LIEU OF TAXES PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should be pleased to answer the question raised in the House by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) on February 20, 1981. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) has managed to solve the problem, and in fact, on December 22, 1981, the Department of Public Works issued a press release which included the following:
The sum of $34,030,000 has been paid to the city of Ottawa as grants in lieu of taxes for 1980. This was announced today by the Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin, Minister of Transport Canada, on behalf of the Hon. Paul Cosgrove, Minister of Public Works Canada.
The amount of the grant, which constitutes an increase of $5,300,000 over 1979, covers all federal property in Ottawa included in the municipal grants program administered by PWC.
When it was announced that the amount of the grant would be increased for 1980, Mr. Pepin said he was pleased that lengthy negotiations by the federal government with the provincial and municipal governments had resulted in an agree-
February 16, 1982

ment on the status of grants in lieu of taxes in Ottawa. According to the British North America Act, federal and provincial property are exempted from property taxes. However, since 1950, federal legislation has provided for payment of grants in lieu of taxes, in order to reimburse municipalities for provision of local services.
In 1980, Parliament passed new legislation on municipal grants, which introduced major changes in the methods for calculating grants, the result being to increase the amounts being paid by the Government of Canada to more than 2,500 municipalities. The new Municipal Grants Act also expanded eligibility of property for the program. A number of properties formerly not affected by the program are now subject to a grant.
In Ottawa, properties that are now covered by the program include the Parliament Buildings, the National Arts Centre, the National Gallery, the National Museums and the National Library and Public Archives building. The Municipal Grants Division, formerly part of the Department of Finance, was transferred to Public Works in 1980. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I may point out that according to the media, the Mayor of Ottawa was very pleased with this announcement.

subtopic: EDUCATION-FEDERAL FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION (B) LEVEL OF FUNDING
EDUCATION-FEDERAL FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION (B) LEVEL OF FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 12, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) came to this House and said that he was going to radically alter the transfers to the provinces under established programs financing act by removing a portion of money called revenue guarantee from transfers to the provinces. That amount of money was originally represented by the minister to be $2.8 billion. This was subsequently revised by the minister in Halifax to $3.2 billion, and, when the provinces got their figures together, they determined that the reduction to the provinces amounted to $4.5 billion. This money goes toward established programs for health, and health concerns which we treat, I suppose, to be our right as Canadians. It also goes toward assistance for post-secondary education.
The question on February 10, which was directed to the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan), was in connection with the post-secondary part of those transfers.
On February 3, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) indicated that there would be no cuts in the transfers she was making. On February 10, I asked the Secretary of State if there would be cuts with respect to post-secondary education. I asked him particularly if the $1.8 billion which he was transferring to the provinces in cash at that time would be increased in the way the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated her transfers would be increased. I was not particularly happy with the answers I
Adjournment Debate
received, because the minister refused to come clean. It is my hope that tonight the parliamentary secretary will come clean.
There is no such thing as "revenue guarantee" in the blue book, the estimates filed for Canada. There has not been such a thing at any time, as far as I know, and certainly not under the terms of present established programs financing. Nowhere does "revenue guarantee" appear. The only place it appears, with respect to the whole problem before us, is in the budget of the Minister of Finance. However, the effect has been to drive concerns on the part of provinces, universities, health care institutions, doctors, and the like. The question must be settled. Is there to be a change in the transfers for post-secondary education and for health care?
The question the parliamentary secretary is to answer tonight is with respect to post-secondary education. Will the parliamentary secretary affirm tonight, in no uncertain language, that the funds which amount to $1,845 billion as set out in the current estimates for this fiscal year, in the manner they are presently transferred in the blue book for post-secondary education, will be escalated in accordance with the arrangements under established programs financing, in accordance with a moving average of GNP? The Secretary of State said that next year those transfers would be escalating approximately 12 per cent, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare said they would be escalating 13.4 per cent. In any event, will those transfers next year be escalated in accordance with the terms of the statute so that the transfers will be escalated in accordance with the moving GNP average?
I point out to the parliamentary secretary that the matter was fully considered by the task force on fiscal arrangements, and four members of the Liberal party, two members of this party, and one member of the New Democratic Party came to some pretty unanimous conclusions with respect to the allocation of moneys to the provinces. I point out that the committee dealt with the question of revenue guarantee and how that component was made up in the original calculations of 1976. The task force clearly indicated that revenue guarantee now formed part of the package for post-secondary education and health care. In particular, the task force stated:
It is our view that there is now ... no fat left in the system-no fat in post-secondary education, no fat in the health system, no excess spending in social assistance, little redundancy in social services. We accept the representations of those who argued before the task force that serious cuts in program funding would cut into muscle and sinew, not fat. Unless one could presume that federal reductions in funding would automatically be matched by corresponding increases in provincial expenditures-a presumption that may not be considered altogether plausible-then in order to maintain present standards, programs would have to be privately financed to a greater extent than at present. In health, this would mean greater appeal to user charges and more extra billing; in education, higher fees. In either case, basic national objectives of equity and equality of access would suffer.
I ask the parliamentary secretary tonight to come clean with the House of Commons, his colleagues on the government side and those on this side on the task force which unanimously recommended to the government that there be no changes in the formulae and that they proceed as they were. These are established programs. They are the programs on which the

February 16, 1982
Adjournment Debate
unity and social services of this country are based. They are based on a contribution by the federal government to postsecondary education, health care, extended health care and a formula in relation to GNP. It is time for the government, not to dance around any longer, but to come clean and tell us if in fact it plans to cut transfers to the provinces or leave them the way they are.
We do not want any gobbledygook about taxes or anything else. We want to know where we stand. Is the government prepared to fulfil the request of the task force, which was unanimous and which was supported by the Economic Council of Canada, or is it going to again dance around and say it is not cutting education, when it is in fact cutting education; not cutting health care, when it is in fact cutting health care; and as it removes certain formulae that it says exist, which in fact do not exist?

Mr. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary
of State): Mr. Speaker, the member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) is referring to the sum of $1.8 billion and expects us to accept word for word the report by the Task Force on Fiscal Arrangements. That is surprising, since he himself is aware the actual amount is closer to $3.2 billion, since his own task force asked us to continue-

-to calculate the equalized value of taxes transferred and that these amounts be earmarked for the program areas. We are talking about $3.2 billion. The hon. member must realize that since November 12 there has been a federal-provincial conference. EPF, whether it is health care or post-secondary education-

-no cuts will be made. And I am sure the hon. member will agree that a 12 per cent increase, given our present economic situation, is quite reasonable. The condition set by the Right Hon. Prime Minister was that the provinces should do their share as well, instead of slacking on their contributions as they have been doing for a number of years. adopted, with which I am sure the hon. member will agree. [English]

subtopic: MINES AND MINING-LOAN TO PERU FOR COPPER MINING VENTURE (B) CREATION OF JOBS IN CANADA
MINES AND MINING-LOAN TO PERU FOR COPPER MINING VENTURE (B) CREATION OF JOBS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question arises from a deal that was struck December 11 between the government and a consortium which I am going to lay before the House tonight. It has been a litany of doubletalk, not only in terms of government policy but what the minister of mines has been telling the general public. The deal was apparently developed by Noranda Mines of Toronto during the past six months. They indicated publicly to at least some bankers that the cost for this deal to break even is about $1 U.S. a pound for the copper to be produced in Peru.
It is interesting that SNC group of Montreal will be supplying the engineering services, the design, the construction and the management for the project which supposedly is going to bring about $100 million of business to Canada, supposedly producing 2,900 person-years of employment. The Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) says 3,000 person-years. The EDC says 2,900 person-years. Neither can demonstrate to the House or to the public what any of those jobs are, even in terms of global categories. Hopefully tonight we will be able to get that from the minister.
The minister says that mine will come into operation in 1987. The EDC and the operators say it will open in about two years, in 1984. That is another discrepancy.
The minister says it will generate about $100 million in Canada, but the real question to which this House has to address itself-and I am sure many mining communities are wondering about this-is why the Government of Canada can lend $100 million to Peru at 11 per cent or less when our mining companies, particularly in the copper industry, from coast to coast are suffering, whether they be in Kamloops, Stewart, Newfoundland, Manitoba or Sudbury, where 850 jobs have just been lost. Those jobs are being lost, because of high interest rates, and because of a lack of capital to carry an inventory of copper or product, or because of a lack of manufacturing, either smelting or secondary processing.
To tie that into general government policy, on February 13 a very interesting government policy was outlined by the economic development minister, Senator Olson. He said;
From here on the national government will invest its capital in areas of prospective growth in the future-
He also said:
We're going to stop propping up mature industries that will never be competitive in this generation, like textiles, clothing, footwear and a number of others.
He went on to say:
We're not going to process every one of our natural resources into the final product. For one thing, we don't have the people. And there are lots of places in the world where they can manufacture products at a much lower cost.
February 16, 1982

That is this government's policy on economic development. The government says, "Do it somewhere else if you can make more money for somebody else."
On February 3 the Minister of State for Mines responded to a question I raised on this very issue. I pointed out that 4,000 jobs were lost in the copper mining and associated industries between the time of the announcement and the time I asked my question two weeks ago. Supposedly 2,900 person-hours of work will be created. We do not know what they are. Perhaps there will be 3,000, but we do not know what they are. Flowever, we know we have already lost 4,000 jobs since the announcement.
I asked the minister, "with the Canadian sector paying roughly double the foreign Liberal rate for capital, why does the minister believe that this kind of loan to foreign competitors is in the best interest of the Canadian copper mining industry?" The reason I asked that question was that the minister's office had informed me that the minister was opposed to this kind of deal. I certainly hope to hear from the minister tonight because she cannot go to one sector and say she is opposed and say to another sector that she is in favour. In Canadian politics and in politics around the world that is called double-talk. The minister answered and said that the loan, and I quote:
-affects a copper mine which will not come into production until roughly four or five years down the road-
That is not agreed to by the EDC.
-by which time we hope the copper situation will have improved and that the prices will have risen considerably. The fact is that that loan produces jobs in Canada immediately-
I hope to hear from the minister tonight what those immediate jobs are within the Canadian context.
The minister gave a response to the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) on December 14 regarding this same deal saying:
Exporting the kinds of machinery and engineering techniques which are being exported is precisely what we should be doing in Canada.
I am somewhat puzzled. The Canadian mining machinery sector had a $1.5 billion deficit just last year. When we are already in a deficit position, I wonder whether we have to pay SNC Engineering from Montreal, whether we have to make a special deal for Noranda and whether we have to make all these special deals in order to export machinery. Perhaps the minister could answer very clearly whether she is in favour or opposed to this deal. She cannot have it both ways. What jobs are being created, where and for how long?
What would the situation be if the $250 million had been invested at 11 per cent in the Canadian copper mining industry, either in smelters or in actual ore extraction? What about the 4,000 jobs that have been lost, and the 850 at Sudbury? There have just been some more lay-offs in Stewart, British Columbia today. There have been lay-offs in Manitoba, in the Yukon at Whitehorse Copper, at Bethlehem Copper, Lornex, Granduc, Campbell Resources, Falconbridge, Gaspe, Asarco and Baie Verte. It is a litany. Our copper mining industry is in
Adjournment Debate
trouble, and the Government of Canada is sending capital out of the country at half the cost that industry can get it here.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MINES AND MINING-LOAN TO PERU FOR COPPER MINING VENTURE (B) CREATION OF JOBS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I would like to clarify a few points. I think the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) is playing loose and fast with some figures. First, I would like to reassure the hon. member that the 850 lay-offs he reported to be taking place in Sudbury are indeed not taking place. That figure has been reduced to something like 250 at the moment, and, through close co-operation with a team from the CEIC, the provincial government and the local union we are convinced that number will be reduced to zero.
As to my opposition to this deal, let me assure the hon. member that I was not opposed to it, whatever he heard from my office. Perhaps he misconstrued the questions that I raised about the deal to be opposition. They were not; in fact, they were questions that every responsible member and every responsible minister asked of the EDC.
I should like to clarify the matter of the $250 million for the benefit of the hon. member for Skeena. The $250 million loaned to the government of Peru for the development of a new copper mine in that country is, in fact, to be provided by a group of 11 commercial banks, two of which are Canadian, at normal commercial interest rates, which leaves a balance of $100 million to be provided by the Export Development Corporation. I should like to assure the hon. member that this $100 million will be provided at normal consensus rate guidelines developed by the OECD, so that reduces the loan considerably.
The key purpose of the EDC loan is to generate export business for Canadian manufacturing and service industries from foreign developments that are expected to proceed, regardless of Canadian involvement. 1 should like to assure the hon. member that whether or not the Canadians he lists were involved in this deal, the deal would go on and the copper would be coming onstream four years from now, I guess. I rather doubt it will be onstream much sooner than that. This is certainly the case with the Tintaya loan.
With respect to jobs created in Canada, SNC Group of Montreal already has Canadians working on the project management, and a number of contracts for Canadian-produced mining equipment are expected to be signed this month. I am sure the hon. member appreciates the fact that these contracts must remain confidential until they are signed. As they become public, let me assure him that I will let him know about them as quickly as I am apprised.
Mining equipment and supplies to be purchased are to come from almost every Canadian province and are expected to create the 2,900 person-years of employment in Canada between now and 1985. Again, I should like to assure the hon. member that only the Canadian content is financed by the EDC-only the Canadian content! Those jobs have to be provided in Canada, or they will not be funded by the EDC.

February 16, 1982
Adjournment Debate
There may be some confusion on the part of the hon. member for Skeena concerning this loan. The Peruvian copper mine in question will be developed for production by the mid-1980s whether or not Canadian financing is provided. In fact, the Export Development Corporation faced very stiff competition in winning the loan package so as to generate the $100 million in Canadian purchases.
This loan constitutes Canadian government Financial and technical assistance and I am sure the hon. member would
agree that it is important to provide this kind of technical assistance to Third World nations in support of long-term Canadian policy toward such nations.
